But ’tis a common proof, That lowliness is young ambition’s ladder, Whereto the climber-upward turns his face; But when he once attains the upmost round, He then unto the ladder turns his back, Looks in the clouds, scorning the base degrees By which he did ascend. So Caesar may; Then lest he may, prevent. And since the quarrel Will bear no colour for the thing he is, Fashion it thus: that what he is, augmented, Would run to these and these extremities: And therefore think him as a serpent’s egg Which hatch’d, would, as his kind grow mischievous; And kill him in the shell.

paras.html: Enter Lucius.
paras.t: Enter Lucius.

paras.html:
LUCIUS. The taper burneth in your closet, sir.
Searching the window for a flint, I found
This paper, thus seal’d up, and I am sure
It did not lie there when I went to bed.
paras.t: The taper burneth in your closet, sir. Searching the window for a flint, I found This paper, thus seal’d up, and I am sure It did not lie there when I went to bed.

paras.html: Gives him the letter.
paras.t: Gives him the letter.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Get you to bed again; it is not day.
Is not tomorrow, boy, the Ides of March?
paras.t: Get you to bed again; it is not day. Is not tomorrow, boy, the Ides of March?

paras.html: LUCIUS. I know not, sir.
paras.t: I know not, sir.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Look in the calendar, and bring me word.
paras.t: Look in the calendar, and bring me word.

paras.html: LUCIUS. I will, sir.
paras.t: I will, sir.

paras.html: Exit.
paras.t: Exit.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. The exhalations, whizzing in the air
Give so much light that I may read by them.
paras.t: The exhalations, whizzing in the air Give so much light that I may read by them.

paras.html: Opens the letter and reads.
paras.t: Opens the letter and reads.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. *Brutus, thou sleep’st: awake and see thyself.
Shall Rome, &c. Speak, strike, redress!*
“Brutus, thou sleep’st: awake!”
Such instigations have been often dropp’d
Where I have took them up.
“Shall Rome, &c.” Thus must I piece it out:
Shall Rome stand under one man’s awe? What, Rome?
My ancestors did from the streets of Rome
The Tarquin drive, when he was call’d a king.
“Speak, strike, redress!” Am I entreated
To speak and strike? O Rome, I make thee promise,
If the redress will follow, thou receivest
Thy full petition at the hand of Brutus.
paras.t: *Brutus, thou sleep’st: awake and see thyself. Shall Rome, &c. Speak, strike, redress!* “Brutus, thou sleep’st: awake!” Such instigations have been often dropp’d Where I have took them up. “Shall Rome, &c.” Thus must I piece it out: Shall Rome stand under one man’s awe? What, Rome? My ancestors did from the streets of Rome The Tarquin drive, when he was call’d a king. “Speak, strike, redress!” Am I entreated To speak and strike? O Rome, I make thee promise, If the redress will follow, thou receivest Thy full petition at the hand of Brutus.

paras.html: Enter Lucius.
paras.t: Enter Lucius.

paras.html: LUCIUS. Sir, March is wasted fifteen days.
paras.t: Sir, March is wasted fifteen days.

paras.html: Knock within.
paras.t: Knock within.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. ’Tis good. Go to the gate, somebody knocks.
paras.t: ’Tis good. Go to the gate, somebody knocks.

paras.html: Exit Lucius.
paras.t: Exit Lucius.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Since Cassius first did whet me against Caesar,
I have not slept.
Between the acting of a dreadful thing
And the first motion, all the interim is
Like a phantasma, or a hideous dream:
The genius and the mortal instruments
Are then in council; and the state of man,
Like to a little kingdom, suffers then
The nature of an insurrection.
paras.t: Since Cassius first did whet me against Caesar, I have not slept. Between the acting of a dreadful thing And the first motion, all the interim is Like a phantasma, or a hideous dream: The genius and the mortal instruments Are then in council; and the state of man, Like to a little kingdom, suffers then The nature of an insurrection.

paras.html: Enter Lucius.
paras.t: Enter Lucius.

paras.html:
LUCIUS. Sir, ’tis your brother Cassius at the door,
Who doth desire to see you.
paras.t: Sir, ’tis your brother Cassius at the door, Who doth desire to see you.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Is he alone?
paras.t: Is he alone?

paras.html: LUCIUS. No, sir, there are moe with him.
paras.t: No, sir, there are moe with him.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Do you know them?
paras.t: Do you know them?

paras.html:
LUCIUS. No, sir, their hats are pluck’d about their ears,
And half their faces buried in their cloaks,
That by no means I may discover them
By any mark of favour.
paras.t: No, sir, their hats are pluck’d about their ears, And half their faces buried in their cloaks, That by no means I may discover them By any mark of favour.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Let ’em enter.
paras.t: Let ’em enter.

paras.html: Exit Lucius.
paras.t: Exit Lucius.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. They are the faction. O conspiracy,
Sham’st thou to show thy dangerous brow by night,
When evils are most free? O, then, by day
Where wilt thou find a cavern dark enough
To mask thy monstrous visage? Seek none, conspiracy;
Hide it in smiles and affability:
For if thou path, thy native semblance on,
Not Erebus itself were dim enough
To hide thee from prevention.
paras.t: They are the faction. O conspiracy, Sham’st thou to show thy dangerous brow by night, When evils are most free? O, then, by day Where wilt thou find a cavern dark enough To mask thy monstrous visage? Seek none, conspiracy; Hide it in smiles and affability: For if thou path, thy native semblance on, Not Erebus itself were dim enough To hide thee from prevention.

paras.html: Enter Cassius, Casca, Decius, Cinna, Metellus Cimber and Trebonius.
paras.t: Enter Cassius, Casca, Decius, Cinna, Metellus Cimber and Trebonius.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. I think we are too bold upon your rest:
Good morrow, Brutus; do we trouble you?
paras.t: I think we are too bold upon your rest: Good morrow, Brutus; do we trouble you?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. I have been up this hour, awake all night.
Know I these men that come along with you?
paras.t: I have been up this hour, awake all night. Know I these men that come along with you?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Yes, every man of them; and no man here
But honours you; and everyone doth wish
You had but that opinion of yourself
Which every noble Roman bears of you.
This is Trebonius.
paras.t: Yes, every man of them; and no man here But honours you; and everyone doth wish You had but that opinion of yourself Which every noble Roman bears of you. This is Trebonius.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. He is welcome hither.
paras.t: He is welcome hither.

paras.html: CASSIUS. This Decius Brutus.
paras.t: This Decius Brutus.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. He is welcome too.
paras.t: He is welcome too.

paras.html: CASSIUS. This, Casca; this, Cinna; and this, Metellus Cimber.
paras.t: This, Casca; this, Cinna; and this, Metellus Cimber.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. They are all welcome.
What watchful cares do interpose themselves
Betwixt your eyes and night?
paras.t: They are all welcome. What watchful cares do interpose themselves Betwixt your eyes and night?

paras.html: CASSIUS. Shall I entreat a word?
paras.t: Shall I entreat a word?

paras.html: They whisper.
paras.t: They whisper.

paras.html: DECIUS BRUTUS. Here lies the east: doth not the day break here?
paras.t: Here lies the east: doth not the day break here?

paras.html: CASCA. No.
paras.t: No.

paras.html:
CINNA. O, pardon, sir, it doth; and yon grey lines
That fret the clouds are messengers of day.
paras.t: O, pardon, sir, it doth; and yon grey lines That fret the clouds are messengers of day.

paras.html:
CASCA. You shall confess that you are both deceiv’d.
Here, as I point my sword, the Sun arises;
Which is a great way growing on the South,
Weighing the youthful season of the year.
Some two months hence, up higher toward the North
He first presents his fire; and the high East
Stands, as the Capitol, directly here.
paras.t: You shall confess that you are both deceiv’d. Here, as I point my sword, the Sun arises; Which is a great way growing on the South, Weighing the youthful season of the year. Some two months hence, up higher toward the North He first presents his fire; and the high East Stands, as the Capitol, directly here.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Give me your hands all over, one by one.
paras.t: Give me your hands all over, one by one.

paras.html: CASSIUS. And let us swear our resolution.
paras.t: And let us swear our resolution.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. No, not an oath. If not the face of men,
The sufferance of our souls, the time’s abuse—
If these be motives weak, break off betimes,
And every man hence to his idle bed.
So let high-sighted tyranny range on,
Till each man drop by lottery. But if these,
As I am sure they do, bear fire enough
To kindle cowards, and to steel with valour
The melting spirits of women; then, countrymen,
What need we any spur but our own cause
To prick us to redress? what other bond
Than secret Romans, that have spoke the word,
And will not palter? and what other oath
Than honesty to honesty engag’d,
That this shall be, or we will fall for it?
Swear priests and cowards, and men cautelous,
Old feeble carrions, and such suffering souls
That welcome wrongs; unto bad causes swear
Such creatures as men doubt; but do not stain
The even virtue of our enterprise,
Nor th’ insuppressive mettle of our spirits,
To think that or our cause or our performance
Did need an oath; when every drop of blood
That every Roman bears, and nobly bears,
Is guilty of a several bastardy,
If he do break the smallest particle
Of any promise that hath pass’d from him.
paras.t: No, not an oath. If not the face of men, The sufferance of our souls, the time’s abuse— If these be motives weak, break off betimes, And every man hence to his idle bed. So let high-sighted tyranny range on, Till each man drop by lottery. But if these, As I am sure they do, bear fire enough To kindle cowards, and to steel with valour The melting spirits of women; then, countrymen, What need we any spur but our own cause To prick us to redress? what other bond Than secret Romans, that have spoke the word, And will not palter? and what other oath Than honesty to honesty engag’d, That this shall be, or we will fall for it? Swear priests and cowards, and men cautelous, Old feeble carrions, and such suffering souls That welcome wrongs; unto bad causes swear Such creatures as men doubt; but do not stain The even virtue of our enterprise, Nor th’ insuppressive mettle of our spirits, To think that or our cause or our performance Did need an oath; when every drop of blood That every Roman bears, and nobly bears, Is guilty of a several bastardy, If he do break the smallest particle Of any promise that hath pass’d from him.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. But what of Cicero? Shall we sound him?
I think he will stand very strong with us.
paras.t: But what of Cicero? Shall we sound him? I think he will stand very strong with us.

paras.html: CASCA. Let us not leave him out.
paras.t: Let us not leave him out.

paras.html: CINNA. No, by no means.
paras.t: No, by no means.

paras.html:
METELLUS CIMBER. O, let us have him, for his silver hairs
Will purchase us a good opinion,
And buy men’s voices to commend our deeds.
It shall be said, his judgement rul’d our hands;
Our youths and wildness shall no whit appear,
But all be buried in his gravity.
paras.t: O, let us have him, for his silver hairs Will purchase us a good opinion, And buy men’s voices to commend our deeds. It shall be said, his judgement rul’d our hands; Our youths and wildness shall no whit appear, But all be buried in his gravity.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. O, name him not; let us not break with him;
For he will never follow anything
That other men begin.
paras.t: O, name him not; let us not break with him; For he will never follow anything That other men begin.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Then leave him out.
paras.t: Then leave him out.

paras.html: CASCA. Indeed, he is not fit.
paras.t: Indeed, he is not fit.

paras.html: DECIUS BRUTUS. Shall no man else be touch’d but only Caesar?
paras.t: Shall no man else be touch’d but only Caesar?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Decius, well urg’d. I think it is not meet,
Mark Antony, so well belov’d of Caesar,
Should outlive Caesar: we shall find of him
A shrewd contriver; and you know, his means,
If he improve them, may well stretch so far
As to annoy us all; which to prevent,
Let Antony and Caesar fall together.
paras.t: Decius, well urg’d. I think it is not meet, Mark Antony, so well belov’d of Caesar, Should outlive Caesar: we shall find of him A shrewd contriver; and you know, his means, If he improve them, may well stretch so far As to annoy us all; which to prevent, Let Antony and Caesar fall together.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Our course will seem too bloody, Caius Cassius,
To cut the head off, and then hack the limbs,
Like wrath in death, and envy afterwards;
For Antony is but a limb of Caesar.
Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius.
We all stand up against the spirit of Caesar,
And in the spirit of men there is no blood.
O, that we then could come by Caesar’s spirit,
And not dismember Caesar! But, alas,
Caesar must bleed for it! And, gentle friends,
Let’s kill him boldly, but not wrathfully;
Let’s carve him as a dish fit for the gods,
Not hew him as a carcass fit for hounds.
And let our hearts, as subtle masters do,
Stir up their servants to an act of rage,
And after seem to chide ’em. This shall mark
Our purpose necessary, and not envious;
Which so appearing to the common eyes,
We shall be call’d purgers, not murderers.
And for Mark Antony, think not of him;
For he can do no more than Caesar’s arm
When Caesar’s head is off.
paras.t: Our course will seem too bloody, Caius Cassius, To cut the head off, and then hack the limbs, Like wrath in death, and envy afterwards; For Antony is but a limb of Caesar. Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius. We all stand up against the spirit of Caesar, And in the spirit of men there is no blood. O, that we then could come by Caesar’s spirit, And not dismember Caesar! But, alas, Caesar must bleed for it! And, gentle friends, Let’s kill him boldly, but not wrathfully; Let’s carve him as a dish fit for the gods, Not hew him as a carcass fit for hounds. And let our hearts, as subtle masters do, Stir up their servants to an act of rage, And after seem to chide ’em. This shall mark Our purpose necessary, and not envious; Which so appearing to the common eyes, We shall be call’d purgers, not murderers. And for Mark Antony, think not of him; For he can do no more than Caesar’s arm When Caesar’s head is off.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Yet I fear him;
For in the ingrafted love he bears to Caesar—
paras.t: Yet I fear him; For in the ingrafted love he bears to Caesar—

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Alas, good Cassius, do not think of him:
If he love Caesar, all that he can do
Is to himself; take thought and die for Caesar.
And that were much he should; for he is given
To sports, to wildness, and much company.
paras.t: Alas, good Cassius, do not think of him: If he love Caesar, all that he can do Is to himself; take thought and die for Caesar. And that were much he should; for he is given To sports, to wildness, and much company.

paras.html:
TREBONIUS. There is no fear in him; let him not die;
For he will live, and laugh at this hereafter.
paras.t: There is no fear in him; let him not die; For he will live, and laugh at this hereafter.

paras.html: Clock strikes.
paras.t: Clock strikes.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Peace! count the clock.
paras.t: Peace! count the clock.

paras.html: CASSIUS. The clock hath stricken three.
paras.t: The clock hath stricken three.

paras.html: TREBONIUS. ’Tis time to part.
paras.t: ’Tis time to part.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. But it is doubtful yet
Whether Caesar will come forth today or no;
For he is superstitious grown of late,
Quite from the main opinion he held once
Of fantasy, of dreams, and ceremonies.
It may be these apparent prodigies,
The unaccustom’d terror of this night,
And the persuasion of his augurers,
May hold him from the Capitol today.
paras.t: But it is doubtful yet Whether Caesar will come forth today or no; For he is superstitious grown of late, Quite from the main opinion he held once Of fantasy, of dreams, and ceremonies. It may be these apparent prodigies, The unaccustom’d terror of this night, And the persuasion of his augurers, May hold him from the Capitol today.

paras.html:
DECIUS BRUTUS. Never fear that: if he be so resolved,
I can o’ersway him, for he loves to hear
That unicorns may be betray’d with trees,
And bears with glasses, elephants with holes,
Lions with toils, and men with flatterers.
But when I tell him he hates flatterers,
He says he does, being then most flattered.
Let me work;
For I can give his humour the true bent,
And I will bring him to the Capitol.
paras.t: Never fear that: if he be so resolved, I can o’ersway him, for he loves to hear That unicorns may be betray’d with trees, And bears with glasses, elephants with holes, Lions with toils, and men with flatterers. But when I tell him he hates flatterers, He says he does, being then most flattered. Let me work; For I can give his humour the true bent, And I will bring him to the Capitol.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Nay, we will all of us be there to fetch him.
paras.t: Nay, we will all of us be there to fetch him.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. By the eighth hour: is that the uttermost?
paras.t: By the eighth hour: is that the uttermost?

paras.html: CINNA. Be that the uttermost; and fail not then.
paras.t: Be that the uttermost; and fail not then.

paras.html:
METELLUS CIMBER. Caius Ligarius doth bear Caesar hard,
Who rated him for speaking well of Pompey;
I wonder none of you have thought of him.
paras.t: Caius Ligarius doth bear Caesar hard, Who rated him for speaking well of Pompey; I wonder none of you have thought of him.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Now, good Metellus, go along by him:
He loves me well, and I have given him reason;
Send him but hither, and I’ll fashion him.
paras.t: Now, good Metellus, go along by him: He loves me well, and I have given him reason; Send him but hither, and I’ll fashion him.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. The morning comes upon’s. We’ll leave you, Brutus.
And, friends, disperse yourselves; but all remember
What you have said, and show yourselves true Romans.
paras.t: The morning comes upon’s. We’ll leave you, Brutus. And, friends, disperse yourselves; but all remember What you have said, and show yourselves true Romans.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Good gentlemen, look fresh and merrily;
Let not our looks put on our purposes,
But bear it as our Roman actors do,
With untired spirits and formal constancy.
And so, good morrow to you everyone.
paras.t: Good gentlemen, look fresh and merrily; Let not our looks put on our purposes, But bear it as our Roman actors do, With untired spirits and formal constancy. And so, good morrow to you everyone.

paras.html: Exeunt all but Brutus.
paras.t: Exeunt all but Brutus.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Boy! Lucius! Fast asleep? It is no matter;
Enjoy the honey-heavy dew of slumber:
Thou hast no figures nor no fantasies,
Which busy care draws in the brains of men;
Therefore thou sleep’st so sound.
paras.t: Boy! Lucius! Fast asleep? It is no matter; Enjoy the honey-heavy dew of slumber: Thou hast no figures nor no fantasies, Which busy care draws in the brains of men; Therefore thou sleep’st so sound.

paras.html: Enter Portia.
paras.t: Enter Portia.

paras.html: PORTIA. Brutus, my lord.
paras.t: Brutus, my lord.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Portia, what mean you? Wherefore rise you now?
It is not for your health thus to commit
Your weak condition to the raw cold morning.
paras.t: Portia, what mean you? Wherefore rise you now? It is not for your health thus to commit Your weak condition to the raw cold morning.

paras.html:
PORTIA. Nor for yours neither. Y’ have ungently, Brutus,
Stole from my bed; and yesternight at supper,
You suddenly arose, and walk’d about,
Musing and sighing, with your arms across;
And when I ask’d you what the matter was,
You star’d upon me with ungentle looks.
I urg’d you further; then you scratch’d your head,
And too impatiently stamp’d with your foot;
Yet I insisted, yet you answer’d not,
But with an angry wafture of your hand
Gave sign for me to leave you. So I did,
Fearing to strengthen that impatience
Which seem’d too much enkindled; and withal
Hoping it was but an effect of humour,
Which sometime hath his hour with every man.
It will not let you eat, nor talk, nor sleep;
And could it work so much upon your shape
As it hath much prevail’d on your condition,
I should not know you, Brutus. Dear my lord,
Make me acquainted with your cause of grief.
paras.t: Nor for yours neither. Y’ have ungently, Brutus, Stole from my bed; and yesternight at supper, You suddenly arose, and walk’d about, Musing and sighing, with your arms across; And when I ask’d you what the matter was, You star’d upon me with ungentle looks. I urg’d you further; then you scratch’d your head, And too impatiently stamp’d with your foot; Yet I insisted, yet you answer’d not, But with an angry wafture of your hand Gave sign for me to leave you. So I did, Fearing to strengthen that impatience Which seem’d too much enkindled; and withal Hoping it was but an effect of humour, Which sometime hath his hour with every man. It will not let you eat, nor talk, nor sleep; And could it work so much upon your shape As it hath much prevail’d on your condition, I should not know you, Brutus. Dear my lord, Make me acquainted with your cause of grief.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. I am not well in health, and that is all.
paras.t: I am not well in health, and that is all.

paras.html:
PORTIA. Brutus is wise, and, were he not in health,
He would embrace the means to come by it.
paras.t: Brutus is wise, and, were he not in health, He would embrace the means to come by it.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Why, so I do. Good Portia, go to bed.
paras.t: Why, so I do. Good Portia, go to bed.

paras.html:
PORTIA. Is Brutus sick, and is it physical
To walk unbraced and suck up the humours
Of the dank morning? What, is Brutus sick,
And will he steal out of his wholesome bed
To dare the vile contagion of the night,
And tempt the rheumy and unpurged air
To add unto his sickness? No, my Brutus;
You have some sick offence within your mind,
Which, by the right and virtue of my place,
I ought to know of: and, upon my knees,
I charm you, by my once commended beauty,
By all your vows of love, and that great vow
Which did incorporate and make us one,
That you unfold to me, your self, your half,
Why you are heavy, and what men tonight
Have had resort to you; for here have been
Some six or seven, who did hide their faces
Even from darkness.
paras.t: Is Brutus sick, and is it physical To walk unbraced and suck up the humours Of the dank morning? What, is Brutus sick, And will he steal out of his wholesome bed To dare the vile contagion of the night, And tempt the rheumy and unpurged air To add unto his sickness? No, my Brutus; You have some sick offence within your mind, Which, by the right and virtue of my place, I ought to know of: and, upon my knees, I charm you, by my once commended beauty, By all your vows of love, and that great vow Which did incorporate and make us one, That you unfold to me, your self, your half, Why you are heavy, and what men tonight Have had resort to you; for here have been Some six or seven, who did hide their faces Even from darkness.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Kneel not, gentle Portia.
paras.t: Kneel not, gentle Portia.

paras.html:
PORTIA. I should not need, if you were gentle Brutus.
Within the bond of marriage, tell me, Brutus,
Is it excepted I should know no secrets
That appertain to you? Am I your self
But, as it were, in sort or limitation,
To keep with you at meals, comfort your bed,
And talk to you sometimes? Dwell I but in the suburbs
Of your good pleasure? If it be no more,
Portia is Brutus’ harlot, not his wife.
paras.t: I should not need, if you were gentle Brutus. Within the bond of marriage, tell me, Brutus, Is it excepted I should know no secrets That appertain to you? Am I your self But, as it were, in sort or limitation, To keep with you at meals, comfort your bed, And talk to you sometimes? Dwell I but in the suburbs Of your good pleasure? If it be no more, Portia is Brutus’ harlot, not his wife.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. You are my true and honourable wife,
As dear to me as are the ruddy drops
That visit my sad heart.
paras.t: You are my true and honourable wife, As dear to me as are the ruddy drops That visit my sad heart.

paras.html:
PORTIA. If this were true, then should I know this secret.
I grant I am a woman; but withal
A woman that Lord Brutus took to wife;
I grant I am a woman; but withal
A woman well reputed, Cato’s daughter.
Think you I am no stronger than my sex,
Being so father’d and so husbanded?
Tell me your counsels, I will not disclose ’em.
I have made strong proof of my constancy,
Giving myself a voluntary wound
Here, in the thigh: can I bear that with patience
And not my husband’s secrets?
paras.t: If this were true, then should I know this secret. I grant I am a woman; but withal A woman that Lord Brutus took to wife; I grant I am a woman; but withal A woman well reputed, Cato’s daughter. Think you I am no stronger than my sex, Being so father’d and so husbanded? Tell me your counsels, I will not disclose ’em. I have made strong proof of my constancy, Giving myself a voluntary wound Here, in the thigh: can I bear that with patience And not my husband’s secrets?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. O ye gods,
Render me worthy of this noble wife!
paras.t: O ye gods, Render me worthy of this noble wife!

paras.html: Knock.
paras.t: Knock.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Hark, hark, one knocks. Portia, go in awhile;
And by and by thy bosom shall partake
The secrets of my heart.
All my engagements I will construe to thee,
All the charactery of my sad brows.
Leave me with haste.
paras.t: Hark, hark, one knocks. Portia, go in awhile; And by and by thy bosom shall partake The secrets of my heart. All my engagements I will construe to thee, All the charactery of my sad brows. Leave me with haste.

paras.html: Exit Portia.
paras.t: Exit Portia.

paras.html: Enter Lucius with Ligarius.
paras.t: Enter Lucius with Ligarius.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Lucius, who’s that knocks?
paras.t: Lucius, who’s that knocks?

paras.html: LUCIUS. Here is a sick man that would speak with you.
paras.t: Here is a sick man that would speak with you.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Caius Ligarius, that Metellus spake of.
Boy, stand aside. Caius Ligarius, how?
paras.t: Caius Ligarius, that Metellus spake of. Boy, stand aside. Caius Ligarius, how?

paras.html: LIGARIUS. Vouchsafe good-morrow from a feeble tongue.
paras.t: Vouchsafe good-morrow from a feeble tongue.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. O, what a time have you chose out, brave Caius,
To wear a kerchief! Would you were not sick!
paras.t: O, what a time have you chose out, brave Caius, To wear a kerchief! Would you were not sick!

paras.html:
LIGARIUS. I am not sick, if Brutus have in hand
Any exploit worthy the name of honour.
paras.t: I am not sick, if Brutus have in hand Any exploit worthy the name of honour.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Such an exploit have I in hand, Ligarius,
Had you a healthful ear to hear of it.
paras.t: Such an exploit have I in hand, Ligarius, Had you a healthful ear to hear of it.

paras.html:
LIGARIUS. By all the gods that Romans bow before,
I here discard my sickness. Soul of Rome!
Brave son, derived from honourable loins!
Thou, like an exorcist, hast conjur’d up
My mortified spirit. Now bid me run,
And I will strive with things impossible,
Yea, get the better of them. What’s to do?
paras.t: By all the gods that Romans bow before, I here discard my sickness. Soul of Rome! Brave son, derived from honourable loins! Thou, like an exorcist, hast conjur’d up My mortified spirit. Now bid me run, And I will strive with things impossible, Yea, get the better of them. What’s to do?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. A piece of work that will make sick men whole.
paras.t: A piece of work that will make sick men whole.

paras.html: LIGARIUS. But are not some whole that we must make sick?
paras.t: But are not some whole that we must make sick?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. That must we also. What it is, my Caius,
I shall unfold to thee, as we are going,
To whom it must be done.
paras.t: That must we also. What it is, my Caius, I shall unfold to thee, as we are going, To whom it must be done.

paras.html:
LIGARIUS. Set on your foot,
And with a heart new-fir’d I follow you,
To do I know not what; but it sufficeth
That Brutus leads me on.
paras.t: Set on your foot, And with a heart new-fir’d I follow you, To do I know not what; but it sufficeth That Brutus leads me on.

paras.html: Thunder.
paras.t: Thunder.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Follow me then.
paras.t: Follow me then.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene II · A room in Caesar’s palace

paras.html: Thunder and lightning. Enter Caesar, in his nightgown.
paras.t: Thunder and lightning. Enter Caesar, in his nightgown.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. Nor heaven nor earth have been at peace tonight: Thrice hath Calphurnia in her sleep cried out, “Help, ho! They murder Caesar!” Who’s within?
paras.t: Nor heaven nor earth have been at peace tonight: Thrice hath Calphurnia in her sleep cried out, “Help, ho! They murder Caesar!” Who’s within?

paras.html: Enter a Servant.
paras.t: Enter a Servant.

paras.html: SERVANT. My lord?
paras.t: My lord?

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. Go bid the priests do present sacrifice,
And bring me their opinions of success.
paras.t: Go bid the priests do present sacrifice, And bring me their opinions of success.

paras.html: SERVANT. I will, my lord.
paras.t: I will, my lord.

paras.html: Exit.
paras.t: Exit.

paras.html: Enter Calphurnia.
paras.t: Enter Calphurnia.

paras.html:
CALPURNIA. What mean you, Caesar? Think you to walk forth?
You shall not stir out of your house today.
paras.t: What mean you, Caesar? Think you to walk forth? You shall not stir out of your house today.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. Caesar shall forth. The things that threaten’d me
Ne’er look’d but on my back; when they shall see
The face of Caesar, they are vanished.
paras.t: Caesar shall forth. The things that threaten’d me Ne’er look’d but on my back; when they shall see The face of Caesar, they are vanished.

paras.html:
CALPURNIA. Caesar, I never stood on ceremonies,
Yet now they fright me. There is one within,
Besides the things that we have heard and seen,
Recounts most horrid sights seen by the watch.
A lioness hath whelped in the streets,
And graves have yawn’d, and yielded up their dead;
Fierce fiery warriors fight upon the clouds
In ranks and squadrons and right form of war,
Which drizzled blood upon the Capitol;
The noise of battle hurtled in the air,
Horses did neigh, and dying men did groan,
And ghosts did shriek and squeal about the streets.
O Caesar, these things are beyond all use,
And I do fear them!
paras.t: Caesar, I never stood on ceremonies, Yet now they fright me. There is one within, Besides the things that we have heard and seen, Recounts most horrid sights seen by the watch. A lioness hath whelped in the streets, And graves have yawn’d, and yielded up their dead; Fierce fiery warriors fight upon the clouds In ranks and squadrons and right form of war, Which drizzled blood upon the Capitol; The noise of battle hurtled in the air, Horses did neigh, and dying men did groan, And ghosts did shriek and squeal about the streets. O Caesar, these things are beyond all use, And I do fear them!

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. What can be avoided
Whose end is purpos’d by the mighty gods?
Yet Caesar shall go forth; for these predictions
Are to the world in general as to Caesar.
paras.t: What can be avoided Whose end is purpos’d by the mighty gods? Yet Caesar shall go forth; for these predictions Are to the world in general as to Caesar.

paras.html:
CALPURNIA. When beggars die, there are no comets seen;
The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes.
paras.t: When beggars die, there are no comets seen; The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. Cowards die many times before their deaths;
The valiant never taste of death but once.
Of all the wonders that I yet have heard,
It seems to me most strange that men should fear,
Seeing that death, a necessary end,
Will come when it will come.
paras.t: Cowards die many times before their deaths; The valiant never taste of death but once. Of all the wonders that I yet have heard, It seems to me most strange that men should fear, Seeing that death, a necessary end, Will come when it will come.

paras.html: Enter Servant.
paras.t: Enter Servant.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. What say the augurers?
paras.t: What say the augurers?

paras.html:
SERVANT. They would not have you to stir forth today.
Plucking the entrails of an offering forth,
They could not find a heart within the beast.
paras.t: They would not have you to stir forth today. Plucking the entrails of an offering forth, They could not find a heart within the beast.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. The gods do this in shame of cowardice:
Caesar should be a beast without a heart
If he should stay at home today for fear.
No, Caesar shall not. Danger knows full well
That Caesar is more dangerous than he.
We are two lions litter’d in one day,
And I the elder and more terrible,
And Caesar shall go forth.
paras.t: The gods do this in shame of cowardice: Caesar should be a beast without a heart If he should stay at home today for fear. No, Caesar shall not. Danger knows full well That Caesar is more dangerous than he. We are two lions litter’d in one day, And I the elder and more terrible, And Caesar shall go forth.

paras.html:
CALPURNIA. Alas, my lord,
Your wisdom is consum’d in confidence.
Do not go forth today: call it my fear
That keeps you in the house, and not your own.
We’ll send Mark Antony to the Senate-house,
And he shall say you are not well today.
Let me upon my knee prevail in this.
paras.t: Alas, my lord, Your wisdom is consum’d in confidence. Do not go forth today: call it my fear That keeps you in the house, and not your own. We’ll send Mark Antony to the Senate-house, And he shall say you are not well today. Let me upon my knee prevail in this.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. Mark Antony shall say I am not well,
And for thy humour, I will stay at home.
paras.t: Mark Antony shall say I am not well, And for thy humour, I will stay at home.

paras.html: Enter Decius.
paras.t: Enter Decius.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. Here’s Decius Brutus, he shall tell them so.
paras.t: Here’s Decius Brutus, he shall tell them so.

paras.html:
DECIUS BRUTUS. Caesar, all hail! Good morrow, worthy Caesar.
I come to fetch you to the Senate-house.
paras.t: Caesar, all hail! Good morrow, worthy Caesar. I come to fetch you to the Senate-house.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. And you are come in very happy time
To bear my greeting to the Senators,
And tell them that I will not come today.
Cannot, is false; and that I dare not, falser:
I will not come today. Tell them so, Decius.
paras.t: And you are come in very happy time To bear my greeting to the Senators, And tell them that I will not come today. Cannot, is false; and that I dare not, falser: I will not come today. Tell them so, Decius.

paras.html: CALPURNIA. Say he is sick.
paras.t: Say he is sick.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. Shall Caesar send a lie?
Have I in conquest stretch’d mine arm so far,
To be afeard to tell grey-beards the truth?
Decius, go tell them Caesar will not come.
paras.t: Shall Caesar send a lie? Have I in conquest stretch’d mine arm so far, To be afeard to tell grey-beards the truth? Decius, go tell them Caesar will not come.

paras.html:
DECIUS BRUTUS. Most mighty Caesar, let me know some cause,
Lest I be laugh’d at when I tell them so.
paras.t: Most mighty Caesar, let me know some cause, Lest I be laugh’d at when I tell them so.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. The cause is in my will; I will not come.
That is enough to satisfy the Senate.
But for your private satisfaction,
Because I love you, I will let you know:
Calphurnia here, my wife, stays me at home.
She dreamt tonight she saw my statue,
Which like a fountain with an hundred spouts
Did run pure blood; and many lusty Romans
Came smiling, and did bathe their hands in it.
And these does she apply for warnings and portents
And evils imminent; and on her knee
Hath begg’d that I will stay at home today.
paras.t: The cause is in my will; I will not come. That is enough to satisfy the Senate. But for your private satisfaction, Because I love you, I will let you know: Calphurnia here, my wife, stays me at home. She dreamt tonight she saw my statue, Which like a fountain with an hundred spouts Did run pure blood; and many lusty Romans Came smiling, and did bathe their hands in it. And these does she apply for warnings and portents And evils imminent; and on her knee Hath begg’d that I will stay at home today.

paras.html:
DECIUS BRUTUS. This dream is all amiss interpreted:
It was a vision fair and fortunate.
Your statue spouting blood in many pipes,
In which so many smiling Romans bath’d,
Signifies that from you great Rome shall suck
Reviving blood, and that great men shall press
For tinctures, stains, relics, and cognizance.
This by Calphurnia’s dream is signified.
paras.t: This dream is all amiss interpreted: It was a vision fair and fortunate. Your statue spouting blood in many pipes, In which so many smiling Romans bath’d, Signifies that from you great Rome shall suck Reviving blood, and that great men shall press For tinctures, stains, relics, and cognizance. This by Calphurnia’s dream is signified.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. And this way have you well expounded it.
paras.t: And this way have you well expounded it.

paras.html:
DECIUS BRUTUS. I have, when you have heard what I can say;
And know it now. The Senate have concluded
To give this day a crown to mighty Caesar.
If you shall send them word you will not come,
Their minds may change. Besides, it were a mock
Apt to be render’d, for someone to say,
“Break up the Senate till another time,
When Caesar’s wife shall meet with better dreams.”
If Caesar hide himself, shall they not whisper
“Lo, Caesar is afraid”?
Pardon me, Caesar; for my dear dear love
To your proceeding bids me tell you this,
And reason to my love is liable.
paras.t: I have, when you have heard what I can say; And know it now. The Senate have concluded To give this day a crown to mighty Caesar. If you shall send them word you will not come, Their minds may change. Besides, it were a mock Apt to be render’d, for someone to say, “Break up the Senate till another time, When Caesar’s wife shall meet with better dreams.” If Caesar hide himself, shall they not whisper “Lo, Caesar is afraid”? Pardon me, Caesar; for my dear dear love To your proceeding bids me tell you this, And reason to my love is liable.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. How foolish do your fears seem now, Calphurnia!
I am ashamed I did yield to them.
Give me my robe, for I will go.
paras.t: How foolish do your fears seem now, Calphurnia! I am ashamed I did yield to them. Give me my robe, for I will go.

paras.html: Enter Brutus, Ligarius, Metellus, Casca, Trebonius, Cinna and Publius.
paras.t: Enter Brutus, Ligarius, Metellus, Casca, Trebonius, Cinna and Publius.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. And look where Publius is come to fetch me.
paras.t: And look where Publius is come to fetch me.

paras.html: PUBLIUS. Good morrow, Caesar.
paras.t: Good morrow, Caesar.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. Welcome, Publius.
What, Brutus, are you stirr’d so early too?
Good morrow, Casca. Caius Ligarius,
Caesar was ne’er so much your enemy
As that same ague which hath made you lean.
What is’t o’clock?
paras.t: Welcome, Publius. What, Brutus, are you stirr’d so early too? Good morrow, Casca. Caius Ligarius, Caesar was ne’er so much your enemy As that same ague which hath made you lean. What is’t o’clock?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Caesar, ’tis strucken eight.
paras.t: Caesar, ’tis strucken eight.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. I thank you for your pains and courtesy.
paras.t: I thank you for your pains and courtesy.

paras.html: Enter Antony.
paras.t: Enter Antony.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. See! Antony, that revels long a-nights,
Is notwithstanding up. Good morrow, Antony.
paras.t: See! Antony, that revels long a-nights, Is notwithstanding up. Good morrow, Antony.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. So to most noble Caesar.
paras.t: So to most noble Caesar.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. Bid them prepare within.
I am to blame to be thus waited for.
Now, Cinna; now, Metellus; what, Trebonius!
I have an hour’s talk in store for you:
Remember that you call on me today;
Be near me, that I may remember you.
paras.t: Bid them prepare within. I am to blame to be thus waited for. Now, Cinna; now, Metellus; what, Trebonius! I have an hour’s talk in store for you: Remember that you call on me today; Be near me, that I may remember you.

paras.html: TREBONIUS. Caesar, I will.
paras.t: Caesar, I will.

paras.html: Aside.
paras.t: Aside.

paras.html:
TREBONIUS. and so near will I be,
That your best friends shall wish I had been further.
paras.t: and so near will I be, That your best friends shall wish I had been further.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. Good friends, go in, and taste some wine with me;
And we, like friends, will straightway go together.
paras.t: Good friends, go in, and taste some wine with me; And we, like friends, will straightway go together.

paras.html: Aside.
paras.t: Aside.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. That every like is not the same, O Caesar,
The heart of Brutus yearns to think upon.
paras.t: That every like is not the same, O Caesar, The heart of Brutus yearns to think upon.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene III · A street near the Capitol

paras.html: Enter Artemidorus, reading a paper.
paras.t: Enter Artemidorus, reading a paper.

paras.html: ARTEMIDORUS. *“Caesar, beware of Brutus; take heed of Cassius; come not near Casca; have an eye to Cinna; trust not Trebonius; mark well Metellus Cimber; Decius Brutus loves thee not; thou hast wrong’d Caius Ligarius. There is but one mind in all these men, and it is bent against Caesar. If thou be’st not immortal, look about you: security gives way to conspiracy. The mighty gods defend thee! Thy lover, Artemidorus.”* Here will I stand till Caesar pass along, And as a suitor will I give him this. My heart laments that virtue cannot live Out of the teeth of emulation. If thou read this, O Caesar, thou mayest live; If not, the Fates with traitors do contrive.

There is but one mind in all these men, and it is bent against Caesar. If thou be’st not immortal, look about you: security gives way to conspiracy. The mighty gods defend thee! Thy lover, Artemidorus.”* Here will I stand till Caesar pass along, And as a suitor will I give him this. My heart laments that virtue cannot live Out of the teeth of emulation. If thou read this, O Caesar, thou mayest live; If not, the Fates with traitors do contrive.

paras.html: Exit.
paras.t: Exit.

chapters.sub: Scene IV · Another part of the same street, before the house of Brutus

paras.html: Enter Portia and Lucius.
paras.t: Enter Portia and Lucius.

paras.html:
PORTIA. I pr’ythee, boy, run to the Senate-house;
Stay not to answer me, but get thee gone.
Why dost thou stay?
paras.t: I pr’ythee, boy, run to the Senate-house; Stay not to answer me, but get thee gone. Why dost thou stay?

paras.html: LUCIUS. To know my errand, madam.
paras.t: To know my errand, madam.

paras.html:
PORTIA. I would have had thee there and here again,
Ere I can tell thee what thou shouldst do there.
paras.t: I would have had thee there and here again, Ere I can tell thee what thou shouldst do there.

paras.html: Aside.
paras.t: Aside.

paras.html:
PORTIA. O constancy, be strong upon my side,
Set a huge mountain ’tween my heart and tongue!
I have a man’s mind, but a woman’s might.
How hard it is for women to keep counsel!
Art thou here yet?
paras.t: O constancy, be strong upon my side, Set a huge mountain ’tween my heart and tongue! I have a man’s mind, but a woman’s might. How hard it is for women to keep counsel! Art thou here yet?

paras.html:
LUCIUS. Madam, what should I do?
Run to the Capitol, and nothing else?
And so return to you, and nothing else?
paras.t: Madam, what should I do? Run to the Capitol, and nothing else? And so return to you, and nothing else?

paras.html:
PORTIA. Yes, bring me word, boy, if thy lord look well,
For he went sickly forth: and take good note
What Caesar doth, what suitors press to him.
Hark, boy, what noise is that?
paras.t: Yes, bring me word, boy, if thy lord look well, For he went sickly forth: and take good note What Caesar doth, what suitors press to him. Hark, boy, what noise is that?

paras.html: LUCIUS. I hear none, madam.
paras.t: I hear none, madam.

paras.html:
PORTIA. Pr’ythee, listen well.
I heard a bustling rumour, like a fray,
And the wind brings it from the Capitol.
paras.t: Pr’ythee, listen well. I heard a bustling rumour, like a fray, And the wind brings it from the Capitol.

paras.html: LUCIUS. Sooth, madam, I hear nothing.
paras.t: Sooth, madam, I hear nothing.

paras.html: Enter the Soothsayer.
paras.t: Enter the Soothsayer.

paras.html:
PORTIA. Come hither, fellow:
Which way hast thou been?
paras.t: Come hither, fellow: Which way hast thou been?

paras.html: SOOTHSAYER. At mine own house, good lady.
paras.t: At mine own house, good lady.

paras.html: PORTIA. What is’t o’clock?
paras.t: What is’t o’clock?

paras.html: SOOTHSAYER. About the ninth hour, lady.
paras.t: About the ninth hour, lady.

paras.html: PORTIA. Is Caesar yet gone to the Capitol?
paras.t: Is Caesar yet gone to the Capitol?

paras.html:
SOOTHSAYER. Madam, not yet. I go to take my stand,
To see him pass on to the Capitol.
paras.t: Madam, not yet. I go to take my stand, To see him pass on to the Capitol.

paras.html: PORTIA. Thou hast some suit to Caesar, hast thou not?
paras.t: Thou hast some suit to Caesar, hast thou not?

paras.html:
SOOTHSAYER. That I have, lady, if it will please Caesar
To be so good to Caesar as to hear me,
I shall beseech him to befriend himself.
paras.t: That I have, lady, if it will please Caesar To be so good to Caesar as to hear me, I shall beseech him to befriend himself.

paras.html: PORTIA. Why, know’st thou any harm’s intended towards him?
paras.t: Why, know’st thou any harm’s intended towards him?

paras.html:
SOOTHSAYER. None that I know will be, much that I fear may chance.
Good morrow to you. Here the street is narrow.
The throng that follows Caesar at the heels,
Of Senators, of Praetors, common suitors,
Will crowd a feeble man almost to death:
I’ll get me to a place more void, and there
Speak to great Caesar as he comes along.
paras.t: None that I know will be, much that I fear may chance. Good morrow to you. Here the street is narrow. The throng that follows Caesar at the heels, Of Senators, of Praetors, common suitors, Will crowd a feeble man almost to death: I’ll get me to a place more void, and there Speak to great Caesar as he comes along.

paras.html: Exit.
paras.t: Exit.

paras.html: PORTIA. I must go in.
paras.t: I must go in.

paras.html: Aside.
paras.t: Aside.

paras.html:
PORTIA. Ay me, how weak a thing
The heart of woman is! O Brutus,
The heavens speed thee in thine enterprise!
Sure, the boy heard me. Brutus hath a suit
That Caesar will not grant. O, I grow faint.
Run, Lucius, and commend me to my lord;
Say I am merry; come to me again,
And bring me word what he doth say to thee.
paras.t: Ay me, how weak a thing The heart of woman is! O Brutus, The heavens speed thee in thine enterprise! Sure, the boy heard me. Brutus hath a suit That Caesar will not grant. O, I grow faint. Run, Lucius, and commend me to my lord; Say I am merry; come to me again, And bring me word what he doth say to thee.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene I · Rome. Before the Capitol; the Senate sitting

paras.html: A crowd of people in the street leading to the Capitol. Flourish. Enter Caesar, Brutus, Cassius, Casca, Decius, Metellus, Trebonius, Cinna, Antony, Lepidus, Artemidorus, Publius, Popilius and the Soothsayer.
paras.t: A crowd of people in the street leading to the Capitol. Flourish. Enter Caesar, Brutus, Cassius, Casca, Decius, Metellus, Trebonius, Cinna, Antony, Lepidus, Artemidorus, Publius, Popilius and the Soothsayer.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. The Ides of March are come.
paras.t: The Ides of March are come.

paras.html: SOOTHSAYER. Ay, Caesar; but not gone.
paras.t: Ay, Caesar; but not gone.

paras.html: ARTEMIDORUS. Hail, Caesar! Read this schedule.
paras.t: Hail, Caesar! Read this schedule.

paras.html:
DECIUS BRUTUS. Trebonius doth desire you to o’er-read,
At your best leisure, this his humble suit.
paras.t: Trebonius doth desire you to o’er-read, At your best leisure, this his humble suit.

paras.html:
ARTEMIDORUS. O Caesar, read mine first; for mine’s a suit
That touches Caesar nearer. Read it, great Caesar.
paras.t: O Caesar, read mine first; for mine’s a suit That touches Caesar nearer. Read it, great Caesar.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. What touches us ourself shall be last serv’d.
paras.t: What touches us ourself shall be last serv’d.

paras.html: ARTEMIDORUS. Delay not, Caesar. Read it instantly.
paras.t: Delay not, Caesar. Read it instantly.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. What, is the fellow mad?
paras.t: What, is the fellow mad?

paras.html: PUBLIUS. Sirrah, give place.
paras.t: Sirrah, give place.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. What, urge you your petitions in the street?
Come to the Capitol.
paras.t: What, urge you your petitions in the street? Come to the Capitol.

paras.html: Caesar enters the Capitol, the rest following. All the Senators rise.
paras.t: Caesar enters the Capitol, the rest following. All the Senators rise.

paras.html: POPILIUS LENA. I wish your enterprise today may thrive.
paras.t: I wish your enterprise today may thrive.

paras.html: CASSIUS. What enterprise, Popilius?
paras.t: What enterprise, Popilius?

paras.html: POPILIUS LENA. Fare you well.
paras.t: Fare you well.

paras.html: Advances to Caesar.
paras.t: Advances to Caesar.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. What said Popilius Lena?
paras.t: What said Popilius Lena?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. He wish’d today our enterprise might thrive.
I fear our purpose is discovered.
paras.t: He wish’d today our enterprise might thrive. I fear our purpose is discovered.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Look how he makes to Caesar: mark him.
paras.t: Look how he makes to Caesar: mark him.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Casca, be sudden, for we fear prevention.
Brutus, what shall be done? If this be known,
Cassius or Caesar never shall turn back,
For I will slay myself.
paras.t: Casca, be sudden, for we fear prevention. Brutus, what shall be done? If this be known, Cassius or Caesar never shall turn back, For I will slay myself.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Cassius, be constant:
Popilius Lena speaks not of our purposes;
For look, he smiles, and Caesar doth not change.
paras.t: Cassius, be constant: Popilius Lena speaks not of our purposes; For look, he smiles, and Caesar doth not change.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Trebonius knows his time, for look you, Brutus,
He draws Mark Antony out of the way.
paras.t: Trebonius knows his time, for look you, Brutus, He draws Mark Antony out of the way.

paras.html: Exeunt Antony and Trebonius. Caesar and the Senators take their seats.
paras.t: Exeunt Antony and Trebonius. Caesar and the Senators take their seats.

paras.html:
DECIUS BRUTUS. Where is Metellus Cimber? Let him go,
And presently prefer his suit to Caesar.
paras.t: Where is Metellus Cimber? Let him go, And presently prefer his suit to Caesar.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. He is address’d; press near and second him.
paras.t: He is address’d; press near and second him.

paras.html: CINNA. Casca, you are the first that rears your hand.
paras.t: Casca, you are the first that rears your hand.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. Are we all ready? What is now amiss
That Caesar and his Senate must redress?
paras.t: Are we all ready? What is now amiss That Caesar and his Senate must redress?

paras.html:
METELLUS CIMBER. Most high, most mighty, and most puissant Caesar,
Metellus Cimber throws before thy seat
An humble heart.
paras.t: Most high, most mighty, and most puissant Caesar, Metellus Cimber throws before thy seat An humble heart.

paras.html: Kneeling.
paras.t: Kneeling.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. I must prevent thee, Cimber.
These couchings and these lowly courtesies
Might fire the blood of ordinary men,
And turn pre-ordinance and first decree
Into the law of children. Be not fond,
To think that Caesar bears such rebel blood
That will be thaw’d from the true quality
With that which melteth fools; I mean sweet words,
Low-crooked curtsies, and base spaniel fawning.
Thy brother by decree is banished:
If thou dost bend, and pray, and fawn for him,
I spurn thee like a cur out of my way.
Know, Caesar dost not wrong, nor without cause
Will he be satisfied.
paras.t: I must prevent thee, Cimber. These couchings and these lowly courtesies Might fire the blood of ordinary men, And turn pre-ordinance and first decree Into the law of children. Be not fond, To think that Caesar bears such rebel blood That will be thaw’d from the true quality With that which melteth fools; I mean sweet words, Low-crooked curtsies, and base spaniel fawning. Thy brother by decree is banished: If thou dost bend, and pray, and fawn for him, I spurn thee like a cur out of my way. Know, Caesar dost not wrong, nor without cause Will he be satisfied.

paras.html:
METELLUS CIMBER. Is there no voice more worthy than my own,
To sound more sweetly in great Caesar’s ear
For the repealing of my banish’d brother?
paras.t: Is there no voice more worthy than my own, To sound more sweetly in great Caesar’s ear For the repealing of my banish’d brother?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. I kiss thy hand, but not in flattery, Caesar;
Desiring thee that Publius Cimber may
Have an immediate freedom of repeal.
paras.t: I kiss thy hand, but not in flattery, Caesar; Desiring thee that Publius Cimber may Have an immediate freedom of repeal.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. What, Brutus?
paras.t: What, Brutus?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Pardon, Caesar; Caesar, pardon:
As low as to thy foot doth Cassius fall,
To beg enfranchisement for Publius Cimber.
paras.t: Pardon, Caesar; Caesar, pardon: As low as to thy foot doth Cassius fall, To beg enfranchisement for Publius Cimber.

paras.html:
JULIUS CAESAR. I could be well mov’d, if I were as you;
If I could pray to move, prayers would move me:
But I am constant as the northern star,
Of whose true-fix’d and resting quality
There is no fellow in the firmament.
The skies are painted with unnumber’d sparks,
They are all fire, and every one doth shine;
But there’s but one in all doth hold his place.
So in the world; ’tis furnish’d well with men,
And men are flesh and blood, and apprehensive;
Yet in the number I do know but one
That unassailable holds on his rank,
Unshak’d of motion: and that I am he,
Let me a little show it, even in this,
That I was constant Cimber should be banish’d,
And constant do remain to keep him so.
paras.t: I could be well mov’d, if I were as you; If I could pray to move, prayers would move me: But I am constant as the northern star, Of whose true-fix’d and resting quality There is no fellow in the firmament. The skies are painted with unnumber’d sparks, They are all fire, and every one doth shine; But there’s but one in all doth hold his place. So in the world; ’tis furnish’d well with men, And men are flesh and blood, and apprehensive; Yet in the number I do know but one That unassailable holds on his rank, Unshak’d of motion: and that I am he, Let me a little show it, even in this, That I was constant Cimber should be banish’d, And constant do remain to keep him so.

paras.html: CINNA. O Caesar,—
paras.t: O Caesar,—

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. Hence! wilt thou lift up Olympus?
paras.t: Hence! wilt thou lift up Olympus?

paras.html: DECIUS BRUTUS. Great Caesar,—
paras.t: Great Caesar,—

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. Doth not Brutus bootless kneel?
paras.t: Doth not Brutus bootless kneel?

paras.html: CASCA. Speak, hands, for me!
paras.t: Speak, hands, for me!

paras.html: Casca stabs Caesar in the neck. Caesar catches hold of his arm. He is then stabbed by several other Conspirators, and at last by Marcus Brutus.
paras.t: Casca stabs Caesar in the neck. Caesar catches hold of his arm. He is then stabbed by several other Conspirators, and at last by Marcus Brutus.

paras.html: JULIUS CAESAR. *Et tu, Brute?*—Then fall, Caesar!
paras.t: *Et tu, Brute?*—Then fall, Caesar!

paras.html: Dies. The Senators and People retire in confusion.
paras.t: Dies. The Senators and People retire in confusion.

paras.html:
CINNA. Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead!
Run hence, proclaim, cry it about the streets.
paras.t: Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead! Run hence, proclaim, cry it about the streets.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Some to the common pulpits and cry out, “Liberty, freedom, and enfranchisement!”
paras.t: Some to the common pulpits and cry out, “Liberty, freedom, and enfranchisement!”

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. People and Senators, be not affrighted.
Fly not; stand still; ambition’s debt is paid.
paras.t: People and Senators, be not affrighted. Fly not; stand still; ambition’s debt is paid.

paras.html: CASCA. Go to the pulpit, Brutus.
paras.t: Go to the pulpit, Brutus.

paras.html: DECIUS BRUTUS. And Cassius too.
paras.t: And Cassius too.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Where’s Publius?
paras.t: Where’s Publius?

paras.html: CINNA. Here, quite confounded with this mutiny.
paras.t: Here, quite confounded with this mutiny.

paras.html:
METELLUS CIMBER. Stand fast together, lest some friend of Caesar’s
Should chance—
paras.t: Stand fast together, lest some friend of Caesar’s Should chance—

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Talk not of standing. Publius, good cheer!
There is no harm intended to your person,
Nor to no Roman else. So tell them, Publius.
paras.t: Talk not of standing. Publius, good cheer! There is no harm intended to your person, Nor to no Roman else. So tell them, Publius.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. And leave us, Publius; lest that the people
Rushing on us, should do your age some mischief.
paras.t: And leave us, Publius; lest that the people Rushing on us, should do your age some mischief.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Do so; and let no man abide this deed
But we the doers.
paras.t: Do so; and let no man abide this deed But we the doers.

paras.html: Enter Trebonius.
paras.t: Enter Trebonius.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Where’s Antony?
paras.t: Where’s Antony?

paras.html:
TREBONIUS. Fled to his house amaz’d.
Men, wives, and children stare, cry out, and run,
As it were doomsday.
paras.t: Fled to his house amaz’d. Men, wives, and children stare, cry out, and run, As it were doomsday.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Fates, we will know your pleasures.
That we shall die, we know; ’tis but the time
And drawing days out, that men stand upon.
paras.t: Fates, we will know your pleasures. That we shall die, we know; ’tis but the time And drawing days out, that men stand upon.

paras.html:
CASCA. Why, he that cuts off twenty years of life
Cuts off so many years of fearing death.
paras.t: Why, he that cuts off twenty years of life Cuts off so many years of fearing death.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Grant that, and then is death a benefit:
So are we Caesar’s friends, that have abridg’d
His time of fearing death. Stoop, Romans, stoop,
And let us bathe our hands in Caesar’s blood
Up to the elbows, and besmear our swords:
Then walk we forth, even to the market-place,
And waving our red weapons o’er our heads,
Let’s all cry, “Peace, freedom, and liberty!”
paras.t: Grant that, and then is death a benefit: So are we Caesar’s friends, that have abridg’d His time of fearing death. Stoop, Romans, stoop, And let us bathe our hands in Caesar’s blood Up to the elbows, and besmear our swords: Then walk we forth, even to the market-place, And waving our red weapons o’er our heads, Let’s all cry, “Peace, freedom, and liberty!”

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Stoop then, and wash. How many ages hence
Shall this our lofty scene be acted over
In States unborn, and accents yet unknown!
paras.t: Stoop then, and wash. How many ages hence Shall this our lofty scene be acted over In States unborn, and accents yet unknown!

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. How many times shall Caesar bleed in sport,
That now on Pompey’s basis lies along,
No worthier than the dust!
paras.t: How many times shall Caesar bleed in sport, That now on Pompey’s basis lies along, No worthier than the dust!

paras.html:
CASSIUS. So oft as that shall be,
So often shall the knot of us be call’d
The men that gave their country liberty.
paras.t: So oft as that shall be, So often shall the knot of us be call’d The men that gave their country liberty.

paras.html: DECIUS BRUTUS. What, shall we forth?
paras.t: What, shall we forth?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Ay, every man away.
Brutus shall lead; and we will grace his heels
With the most boldest and best hearts of Rome.
paras.t: Ay, every man away. Brutus shall lead; and we will grace his heels With the most boldest and best hearts of Rome.

paras.html: Enter a Servant.
paras.t: Enter a Servant.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Soft, who comes here? A friend of Antony’s.
paras.t: Soft, who comes here? A friend of Antony’s.

paras.html:
SERVANT. Thus, Brutus, did my master bid me kneel;
Thus did Mark Antony bid me fall down;
And, being prostrate, thus he bade me say:
Brutus is noble, wise, valiant, and honest;
Caesar was mighty, bold, royal, and loving;
Say I love Brutus and I honour him;
Say I fear’d Caesar, honour’d him, and lov’d him.
If Brutus will vouchsafe that Antony
May safely come to him, and be resolv’d
How Caesar hath deserv’d to lie in death,
Mark Antony shall not love Caesar dead
So well as Brutus living; but will follow
The fortunes and affairs of noble Brutus
Thorough the hazards of this untrod state,
With all true faith. So says my master Antony.
paras.t: Thus, Brutus, did my master bid me kneel; Thus did Mark Antony bid me fall down; And, being prostrate, thus he bade me say: Brutus is noble, wise, valiant, and honest; Caesar was mighty, bold, royal, and loving; Say I love Brutus and I honour him; Say I fear’d Caesar, honour’d him, and lov’d him. If Brutus will vouchsafe that Antony May safely come to him, and be resolv’d How Caesar hath deserv’d to lie in death, Mark Antony shall not love Caesar dead So well as Brutus living; but will follow The fortunes and affairs of noble Brutus Thorough the hazards of this untrod state, With all true faith. So says my master Antony.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Thy master is a wise and valiant Roman;
I never thought him worse.
Tell him, so please him come unto this place,
He shall be satisfied and, by my honour,
Depart untouch’d.
paras.t: Thy master is a wise and valiant Roman; I never thought him worse. Tell him, so please him come unto this place, He shall be satisfied and, by my honour, Depart untouch’d.

paras.html: SERVANT. I’ll fetch him presently.
paras.t: I’ll fetch him presently.

paras.html: Exit.
paras.t: Exit.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. I know that we shall have him well to friend.
paras.t: I know that we shall have him well to friend.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. I wish we may: but yet have I a mind
That fears him much; and my misgiving still
Falls shrewdly to the purpose.
paras.t: I wish we may: but yet have I a mind That fears him much; and my misgiving still Falls shrewdly to the purpose.

paras.html: Enter Antony.
paras.t: Enter Antony.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. But here comes Antony. Welcome, Mark Antony.
paras.t: But here comes Antony. Welcome, Mark Antony.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. O mighty Caesar! Dost thou lie so low?
Are all thy conquests, glories, triumphs, spoils,
Shrunk to this little measure? Fare thee well.
I know not, gentlemen, what you intend,
Who else must be let blood, who else is rank:
If I myself, there is no hour so fit
As Caesar’s death’s hour; nor no instrument
Of half that worth as those your swords, made rich
With the most noble blood of all this world.
I do beseech ye, if you bear me hard,
Now, whilst your purpled hands do reek and smoke,
Fulfill your pleasure. Live a thousand years,
I shall not find myself so apt to die.
No place will please me so, no means of death,
As here by Caesar, and by you cut off,
The choice and master spirits of this age.
paras.t: O mighty Caesar! Dost thou lie so low? Are all thy conquests, glories, triumphs, spoils, Shrunk to this little measure? Fare thee well. I know not, gentlemen, what you intend, Who else must be let blood, who else is rank: If I myself, there is no hour so fit As Caesar’s death’s hour; nor no instrument Of half that worth as those your swords, made rich With the most noble blood of all this world. I do beseech ye, if you bear me hard, Now, whilst your purpled hands do reek and smoke, Fulfill your pleasure. Live a thousand years, I shall not find myself so apt to die. No place will please me so, no means of death, As here by Caesar, and by you cut off, The choice and master spirits of this age.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. O Antony, beg not your death of us.
Though now we must appear bloody and cruel,
As by our hands and this our present act
You see we do; yet see you but our hands
And this the bleeding business they have done.
Our hearts you see not; they are pitiful;
And pity to the general wrong of Rome—
As fire drives out fire, so pity pity—
Hath done this deed on Caesar. For your part,
To you our swords have leaden points, Mark Antony;
Our arms in strength of malice, and our hearts
Of brothers’ temper, do receive you in
With all kind love, good thoughts, and reverence.
paras.t: O Antony, beg not your death of us. Though now we must appear bloody and cruel, As by our hands and this our present act You see we do; yet see you but our hands And this the bleeding business they have done. Our hearts you see not; they are pitiful; And pity to the general wrong of Rome— As fire drives out fire, so pity pity— Hath done this deed on Caesar. For your part, To you our swords have leaden points, Mark Antony; Our arms in strength of malice, and our hearts Of brothers’ temper, do receive you in With all kind love, good thoughts, and reverence.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Your voice shall be as strong as any man’s
In the disposing of new dignities.
paras.t: Your voice shall be as strong as any man’s In the disposing of new dignities.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Only be patient till we have appeas’d
The multitude, beside themselves with fear,
And then we will deliver you the cause
Why I, that did love Caesar when I struck him,
Have thus proceeded.
paras.t: Only be patient till we have appeas’d The multitude, beside themselves with fear, And then we will deliver you the cause Why I, that did love Caesar when I struck him, Have thus proceeded.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. I doubt not of your wisdom.
Let each man render me his bloody hand.
First, Marcus Brutus, will I shake with you;
Next, Caius Cassius, do I take your hand.
Now, Decius Brutus, yours; now yours, Metellus;
Yours, Cinna; and, my valiant Casca, yours;
Though last, not least in love, yours, good Trebonius.
Gentlemen all—alas, what shall I say?
My credit now stands on such slippery ground,
That one of two bad ways you must conceit me,
Either a coward or a flatterer.
That I did love thee, Caesar, O, ’tis true:
If then thy spirit look upon us now,
Shall it not grieve thee dearer than thy death,
To see thy Antony making his peace,
Shaking the bloody fingers of thy foes,
Most noble, in the presence of thy corse?
Had I as many eyes as thou hast wounds,
Weeping as fast as they stream forth thy blood,
It would become me better than to close
In terms of friendship with thine enemies.
Pardon me, Julius! Here wast thou bay’d, brave hart;
Here didst thou fall; and here thy hunters stand,
Sign’d in thy spoil, and crimson’d in thy lethe.
O world, thou wast the forest to this hart;
And this indeed, O world, the heart of thee.
How like a deer strucken by many princes,
Dost thou here lie!

Now, Decius Brutus, yours; now yours, Metellus; Yours, Cinna; and, my valiant Casca, yours; Though last, not least in love, yours, good Trebonius. Gentlemen all—alas, what shall I say? My credit now stands on such slippery ground, That one of two bad ways you must conceit me, Either a coward or a flatterer. That I did love thee, Caesar, O, ’tis true: If then thy spirit look upon us now, Shall it not grieve thee dearer than thy death, To see thy Antony making his peace, Shaking the bloody fingers of thy foes, Most noble, in the presence of thy corse? Had I as many eyes as thou hast wounds, Weeping as fast as they stream forth thy blood, It would become me better than to close In terms of friendship with thine enemies. Pardon me, Julius! Here wast thou bay’d, brave hart; Here didst thou fall; and here thy hunters stand, Sign’d in thy spoil, and crimson’d in thy lethe. O world, thou wast the forest to this hart; And this indeed, O world, the heart of thee. How like a deer strucken by many princes, Dost thou here lie!

paras.html: CASSIUS. Mark Antony,—
paras.t: Mark Antony,—

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Pardon me, Caius Cassius:
The enemies of Caesar shall say this;
Then, in a friend, it is cold modesty.
paras.t: Pardon me, Caius Cassius: The enemies of Caesar shall say this; Then, in a friend, it is cold modesty.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. I blame you not for praising Caesar so;
But what compact mean you to have with us?
Will you be prick’d in number of our friends,
Or shall we on, and not depend on you?
paras.t: I blame you not for praising Caesar so; But what compact mean you to have with us? Will you be prick’d in number of our friends, Or shall we on, and not depend on you?

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Therefore I took your hands; but was indeed
Sway’d from the point, by looking down on Caesar.
Friends am I with you all, and love you all,
Upon this hope, that you shall give me reasons
Why, and wherein, Caesar was dangerous.
paras.t: Therefore I took your hands; but was indeed Sway’d from the point, by looking down on Caesar. Friends am I with you all, and love you all, Upon this hope, that you shall give me reasons Why, and wherein, Caesar was dangerous.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Or else were this a savage spectacle.
Our reasons are so full of good regard
That were you, Antony, the son of Caesar,
You should be satisfied.
paras.t: Or else were this a savage spectacle. Our reasons are so full of good regard That were you, Antony, the son of Caesar, You should be satisfied.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. That’s all I seek,
And am moreover suitor that I may
Produce his body to the market-place;
And in the pulpit, as becomes a friend,
Speak in the order of his funeral.
paras.t: That’s all I seek, And am moreover suitor that I may Produce his body to the market-place; And in the pulpit, as becomes a friend, Speak in the order of his funeral.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. You shall, Mark Antony.
paras.t: You shall, Mark Antony.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Brutus, a word with you.
paras.t: Brutus, a word with you.

paras.html: Aside to Brutus.
paras.t: Aside to Brutus.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. You know not what you do. Do not consent
That Antony speak in his funeral.
Know you how much the people may be mov’d
By that which he will utter?
paras.t: You know not what you do. Do not consent That Antony speak in his funeral. Know you how much the people may be mov’d By that which he will utter?

paras.html: Aside to Cassius.
paras.t: Aside to Cassius.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. By your pardon:
I will myself into the pulpit first,
And show the reason of our Caesar’s death.
What Antony shall speak, I will protest
He speaks by leave and by permission;
And that we are contented Caesar shall
Have all true rights and lawful ceremonies.
It shall advantage more than do us wrong.
paras.t: By your pardon: I will myself into the pulpit first, And show the reason of our Caesar’s death. What Antony shall speak, I will protest He speaks by leave and by permission; And that we are contented Caesar shall Have all true rights and lawful ceremonies. It shall advantage more than do us wrong.

paras.html: Aside to Brutus.
paras.t: Aside to Brutus.

paras.html: CASSIUS. I know not what may fall; I like it not.
paras.t: I know not what may fall; I like it not.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Mark Antony, here, take you Caesar’s body.
You shall not in your funeral speech blame us,
But speak all good you can devise of Caesar,
And say you do’t by our permission;
Else shall you not have any hand at all
About his funeral. And you shall speak
In the same pulpit whereto I am going,
After my speech is ended.
paras.t: Mark Antony, here, take you Caesar’s body. You shall not in your funeral speech blame us, But speak all good you can devise of Caesar, And say you do’t by our permission; Else shall you not have any hand at all About his funeral. And you shall speak In the same pulpit whereto I am going, After my speech is ended.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Be it so;
I do desire no more.
paras.t: Be it so; I do desire no more.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Prepare the body, then, and follow us.
paras.t: Prepare the body, then, and follow us.

paras.html: Exeunt all but Antony.
paras.t: Exeunt all but Antony.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. O, pardon me, thou bleeding piece of earth,
That I am meek and gentle with these butchers.
Thou art the ruins of the noblest man
That ever lived in the tide of times.
Woe to the hand that shed this costly blood!
Over thy wounds now do I prophesy,
Which, like dumb mouths do ope their ruby lips
To beg the voice and utterance of my tongue,
A curse shall light upon the limbs of men;
Domestic fury and fierce civil strife
Shall cumber all the parts of Italy;
Blood and destruction shall be so in use,
And dreadful objects so familiar,
That mothers shall but smile when they behold
Their infants quartered with the hands of war;
All pity chok’d with custom of fell deeds:
And Caesar’s spirit, ranging for revenge,
With Ate by his side come hot from Hell,
Shall in these confines with a monarch’s voice
Cry havoc and let slip the dogs of war,
That this foul deed shall smell above the earth
With carrion men, groaning for burial.

paras.html: Enter a Servant.
paras.t: Enter a Servant.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. You serve Octavius Caesar, do you not?
paras.t: You serve Octavius Caesar, do you not?

paras.html: SERVANT. I do, Mark Antony.
paras.t: I do, Mark Antony.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Caesar did write for him to come to Rome.
paras.t: Caesar did write for him to come to Rome.

paras.html:
SERVANT. He did receive his letters, and is coming,
And bid me say to you by word of mouth,—
paras.t: He did receive his letters, and is coming, And bid me say to you by word of mouth,—

paras.html: Seeing the body.
paras.t: Seeing the body.

paras.html: SERVANT. O Caesar!
paras.t: O Caesar!

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Thy heart is big, get thee apart and weep.
Passion, I see, is catching; for mine eyes,
Seeing those beads of sorrow stand in thine,
Began to water. Is thy master coming?
paras.t: Thy heart is big, get thee apart and weep. Passion, I see, is catching; for mine eyes, Seeing those beads of sorrow stand in thine, Began to water. Is thy master coming?

paras.html: SERVANT. He lies tonight within seven leagues of Rome.
paras.t: He lies tonight within seven leagues of Rome.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Post back with speed, and tell him what hath chanc’d.
Here is a mourning Rome, a dangerous Rome,
No Rome of safety for Octavius yet.
Hie hence, and tell him so. Yet stay awhile;
Thou shalt not back till I have borne this corse
Into the market-place: there shall I try,
In my oration, how the people take
The cruel issue of these bloody men;
According to the which thou shalt discourse
To young Octavius of the state of things.
Lend me your hand.
paras.t: Post back with speed, and tell him what hath chanc’d. Here is a mourning Rome, a dangerous Rome, No Rome of safety for Octavius yet. Hie hence, and tell him so. Yet stay awhile; Thou shalt not back till I have borne this corse Into the market-place: there shall I try, In my oration, how the people take The cruel issue of these bloody men; According to the which thou shalt discourse To young Octavius of the state of things. Lend me your hand.

paras.html: Exeunt with Caesar’s body.
paras.t: Exeunt with Caesar’s body.

chapters.sub: Scene II · The same. The Forum

paras.html: Enter Brutus and goes into the pulpit, and Cassius, with a throng of Citizens.
paras.t: Enter Brutus and goes into the pulpit, and Cassius, with a throng of Citizens.

paras.html: CITIZENS. We will be satisfied; let us be satisfied.
paras.t: We will be satisfied; let us be satisfied.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Then follow me, and give me audience, friends.
Cassius, go you into the other street
And part the numbers.
Those that will hear me speak, let ’em stay here;
Those that will follow Cassius, go with him;
And public reasons shall be rendered
Of Caesar’s death.
paras.t: Then follow me, and give me audience, friends. Cassius, go you into the other street And part the numbers. Those that will hear me speak, let ’em stay here; Those that will follow Cassius, go with him; And public reasons shall be rendered Of Caesar’s death.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. I will hear Brutus speak.
paras.t: I will hear Brutus speak.

paras.html:
SECOND CITIZEN. I will hear Cassius; and compare their reasons,
When severally we hear them rendered.
paras.t: I will hear Cassius; and compare their reasons, When severally we hear them rendered.

paras.html: Exit Cassius, with some of the Citizens. Brutus goes into the rostrum.
paras.t: Exit Cassius, with some of the Citizens. Brutus goes into the rostrum.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. The noble Brutus is ascended: silence!
paras.t: The noble Brutus is ascended: silence!

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Be patient till the last. Romans, countrymen, and lovers, hear me for my cause; and be silent, that you may hear. Believe me for mine honour, and have respect to mine honour, that you may believe. Censure me in your wisdom, and awake your senses, that you may the better judge. If there be any in this assembly, any dear friend of Caesar’s, to him I say that Brutus’ love to Caesar was no less than his. If then that friend demand why Brutus rose against Caesar, this is my answer: Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more. Had you rather Caesar were living, and die all slaves, than that Caesar were dead, to live all free men? As Caesar loved me, I weep for him; as he was fortunate, I rejoice at it; as he was valiant, I honour him; but, as he was ambitious, I slew him. There is tears, for his love; joy for his fortune; honour for his valour; and death, for his ambition. Who is here so base, that would be a bondman? If any, speak; for him have I offended. Who is here so rude, that would not be a Roman? If any, speak; for him have I offended. Who is here so vile, that will not love his country? If any, speak; for him have I offended. I pause for a reply.
