I pause for a reply.

paras.html: CITIZENS. None, Brutus, none.
paras.t: None, Brutus, none.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Then none have I offended. I have done no more to Caesar than you shall do to Brutus. The question of his death is enroll’d in the Capitol, his glory not extenuated, wherein he was worthy; nor his offences enforc’d, for which he suffered death.
paras.t: Then none have I offended. I have done no more to Caesar than you shall do to Brutus. The question of his death is enroll’d in the Capitol, his glory not extenuated, wherein he was worthy; nor his offences enforc’d, for which he suffered death.

paras.html: Enter Antony and others, with Caesar’s body.
paras.t: Enter Antony and others, with Caesar’s body.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Here comes his body, mourned by Mark Antony, who, though he had no hand in his death, shall receive the benefit of his dying, a place in the commonwealth; as which of you shall not? With this I depart, that, as I slew my best lover for the good of Rome, I have the same dagger for myself, when it shall please my country to need my death.
paras.t: Here comes his body, mourned by Mark Antony, who, though he had no hand in his death, shall receive the benefit of his dying, a place in the commonwealth; as which of you shall not? With this I depart, that, as I slew my best lover for the good of Rome, I have the same dagger for myself, when it shall please my country to need my death.

paras.html: CITIZENS. Live, Brutus! live, live!
paras.t: Live, Brutus! live, live!

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. Bring him with triumph home unto his house.
paras.t: Bring him with triumph home unto his house.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Give him a statue with his ancestors.
paras.t: Give him a statue with his ancestors.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. Let him be Caesar.
paras.t: Let him be Caesar.

paras.html:
FOURTH CITIZEN. Caesar’s better parts
Shall be crown’d in Brutus.
paras.t: Caesar’s better parts Shall be crown’d in Brutus.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. We’ll bring him to his house with shouts and clamours.
paras.t: We’ll bring him to his house with shouts and clamours.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. My countrymen,—
paras.t: My countrymen,—

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Peace! Silence! Brutus speaks.
paras.t: Peace! Silence! Brutus speaks.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. Peace, ho!
paras.t: Peace, ho!

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Good countrymen, let me depart alone,
And, for my sake, stay here with Antony.
Do grace to Caesar’s corpse, and grace his speech
Tending to Caesar’s glories, which Mark Antony,
By our permission, is allow’d to make.
I do entreat you, not a man depart,
Save I alone, till Antony have spoke.
paras.t: Good countrymen, let me depart alone, And, for my sake, stay here with Antony. Do grace to Caesar’s corpse, and grace his speech Tending to Caesar’s glories, which Mark Antony, By our permission, is allow’d to make. I do entreat you, not a man depart, Save I alone, till Antony have spoke.

paras.html: Exit.
paras.t: Exit.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. Stay, ho! and let us hear Mark Antony.
paras.t: Stay, ho! and let us hear Mark Antony.

paras.html:
THIRD CITIZEN. Let him go up into the public chair.
We’ll hear him. Noble Antony, go up.
paras.t: Let him go up into the public chair. We’ll hear him. Noble Antony, go up.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. For Brutus’ sake, I am beholding to you.
paras.t: For Brutus’ sake, I am beholding to you.

paras.html: Goes up.
paras.t: Goes up.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. What does he say of Brutus?
paras.t: What does he say of Brutus?

paras.html:
THIRD CITIZEN. He says, for Brutus’ sake
He finds himself beholding to us all.
paras.t: He says, for Brutus’ sake He finds himself beholding to us all.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. ’Twere best he speak no harm of Brutus here!
paras.t: ’Twere best he speak no harm of Brutus here!

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. This Caesar was a tyrant.
paras.t: This Caesar was a tyrant.

paras.html:
THIRD CITIZEN. Nay, that’s certain.
We are blest that Rome is rid of him.
paras.t: Nay, that’s certain. We are blest that Rome is rid of him.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Peace! let us hear what Antony can say.
paras.t: Peace! let us hear what Antony can say.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. You gentle Romans,—
paras.t: You gentle Romans,—

paras.html: CITIZENS. Peace, ho! let us hear him.
paras.t: Peace, ho! let us hear him.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears;
I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him.
The evil that men do lives after them,
The good is oft interred with their bones;
So let it be with Caesar. The noble Brutus
Hath told you Caesar was ambitious.
If it were so, it was a grievous fault,
And grievously hath Caesar answer’d it.
Here, under leave of Brutus and the rest,
For Brutus is an honourable man,
So are they all, all honourable men,
Come I to speak in Caesar’s funeral.
He was my friend, faithful and just to me;
But Brutus says he was ambitious,
And Brutus is an honourable man.
He hath brought many captives home to Rome,
Whose ransoms did the general coffers fill:
Did this in Caesar seem ambitious?
When that the poor have cried, Caesar hath wept;
Ambition should be made of sterner stuff:
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;
And Brutus is an honourable man.
You all did see that on the Lupercal
I thrice presented him a kingly crown,
Which he did thrice refuse. Was this ambition?
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;
And sure he is an honourable man.
I speak not to disprove what Brutus spoke,
But here I am to speak what I do know.
You all did love him once, not without cause;
What cause withholds you then to mourn for him?
O judgement, thou art fled to brutish beasts,
And men have lost their reason. Bear with me.
My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar,
And I must pause till it come back to me.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. Methinks there is much reason in his sayings.
paras.t: Methinks there is much reason in his sayings.

paras.html:
SECOND CITIZEN. If thou consider rightly of the matter,
Caesar has had great wrong.
paras.t: If thou consider rightly of the matter, Caesar has had great wrong.

paras.html:
THIRD CITIZEN. Has he, masters?
I fear there will a worse come in his place.
paras.t: Has he, masters? I fear there will a worse come in his place.

paras.html:
FOURTH CITIZEN. Mark’d ye his words? He would not take the crown;
Therefore ’tis certain he was not ambitious.
paras.t: Mark’d ye his words? He would not take the crown; Therefore ’tis certain he was not ambitious.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. If it be found so, some will dear abide it.
paras.t: If it be found so, some will dear abide it.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Poor soul, his eyes are red as fire with weeping.
paras.t: Poor soul, his eyes are red as fire with weeping.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. There’s not a nobler man in Rome than Antony.
paras.t: There’s not a nobler man in Rome than Antony.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. Now mark him; he begins again to speak.
paras.t: Now mark him; he begins again to speak.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. But yesterday the word of Caesar might
Have stood against the world; now lies he there,
And none so poor to do him reverence.
O masters! If I were dispos’d to stir
Your hearts and minds to mutiny and rage,
I should do Brutus wrong and Cassius wrong,
Who, you all know, are honourable men.
I will not do them wrong; I rather choose
To wrong the dead, to wrong myself and you,
Than I will wrong such honourable men.
But here’s a parchment with the seal of Caesar,
I found it in his closet; ’tis his will:
Let but the commons hear this testament,
Which, pardon me, I do not mean to read,
And they would go and kiss dead Caesar’s wounds,
And dip their napkins in his sacred blood;
Yea, beg a hair of him for memory,
And, dying, mention it within their wills,
Bequeathing it as a rich legacy
Unto their issue.

If I were dispos’d to stir Your hearts and minds to mutiny and rage, I should do Brutus wrong and Cassius wrong, Who, you all know, are honourable men. I will not do them wrong; I rather choose To wrong the dead, to wrong myself and you, Than I will wrong such honourable men. But here’s a parchment with the seal of Caesar, I found it in his closet; ’tis his will: Let but the commons hear this testament, Which, pardon me, I do not mean to read, And they would go and kiss dead Caesar’s wounds, And dip their napkins in his sacred blood; Yea, beg a hair of him for memory, And, dying, mention it within their wills, Bequeathing it as a rich legacy Unto their issue.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. We’ll hear the will. Read it, Mark Antony.
paras.t: We’ll hear the will. Read it, Mark Antony.

paras.html: CITIZENS. The will, the will! We will hear Caesar’s will.
paras.t: The will, the will! We will hear Caesar’s will.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Have patience, gentle friends, I must not read it.
It is not meet you know how Caesar loved you.
You are not wood, you are not stones, but men;
And being men, hearing the will of Caesar,
It will inflame you, it will make you mad.
’Tis good you know not that you are his heirs;
For if you should, O, what would come of it?

You are not wood, you are not stones, but men; And being men, hearing the will of Caesar, It will inflame you, it will make you mad. ’Tis good you know not that you are his heirs; For if you should, O, what would come of it?

paras.html:
FOURTH CITIZEN. Read the will! We’ll hear it, Antony;
You shall read us the will, Caesar’s will!
paras.t: Read the will! We’ll hear it, Antony; You shall read us the will, Caesar’s will!

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Will you be patient? Will you stay awhile?
I have o’ershot myself to tell you of it.
I fear I wrong the honourable men
Whose daggers have stabb’d Caesar; I do fear it.
paras.t: Will you be patient? Will you stay awhile? I have o’ershot myself to tell you of it. I fear I wrong the honourable men Whose daggers have stabb’d Caesar; I do fear it.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. They were traitors. Honourable men!
paras.t: They were traitors. Honourable men!

paras.html: CITIZENS. The will! The testament!
paras.t: The will! The testament!

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. They were villains, murderers. The will! Read the will!
paras.t: They were villains, murderers. The will! Read the will!

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. You will compel me then to read the will?
Then make a ring about the corpse of Caesar,
And let me show you him that made the will.
Shall I descend? and will you give me leave?
paras.t: You will compel me then to read the will? Then make a ring about the corpse of Caesar, And let me show you him that made the will. Shall I descend? and will you give me leave?

paras.html: CITIZENS. Come down.
paras.t: Come down.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Descend.
paras.t: Descend.

paras.html: He comes down.
paras.t: He comes down.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. You shall have leave.
paras.t: You shall have leave.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. A ring! Stand round.
paras.t: A ring! Stand round.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. Stand from the hearse, stand from the body.
paras.t: Stand from the hearse, stand from the body.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Room for Antony, most noble Antony!
paras.t: Room for Antony, most noble Antony!

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Nay, press not so upon me; stand far off.
paras.t: Nay, press not so upon me; stand far off.

paras.html: CITIZENS. Stand back; room! bear back.
paras.t: Stand back; room! bear back.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. If you have tears, prepare to shed them now.
You all do know this mantle. I remember
The first time ever Caesar put it on;
’Twas on a Summer’s evening, in his tent,
That day he overcame the Nervii.
Look, in this place ran Cassius’ dagger through:
See what a rent the envious Casca made:
Through this the well-beloved Brutus stabb’d;
And as he pluck’d his cursed steel away,
Mark how the blood of Caesar follow’d it,
As rushing out of doors, to be resolv’d
If Brutus so unkindly knock’d, or no;
For Brutus, as you know, was Caesar’s angel.
Judge, O you gods, how dearly Caesar lov’d him.
This was the most unkindest cut of all;
For when the noble Caesar saw him stab,
Ingratitude, more strong than traitors’ arms,
Quite vanquish’d him: then burst his mighty heart;
And in his mantle muffling up his face,
Even at the base of Pompey’s statue
Which all the while ran blood, great Caesar fell.
O, what a fall was there, my countrymen!
Then I, and you, and all of us fell down,
Whilst bloody treason flourish’d over us.
O, now you weep; and I perceive you feel
The dint of pity. These are gracious drops.
Kind souls, what weep you when you but behold
Our Caesar’s vesture wounded? Look you here,
Here is himself, marr’d, as you see, with traitors.
paras.t: If you have tears, prepare to shed them now. You all do know this mantle. I remember The first time ever Caesar put it on; ’Twas on a Summer’s evening, in his tent, That day he overcame the Nervii. Look, in this place ran Cassius’ dagger through: See what a rent the envious Casca made: Through this the well-beloved Brutus stabb’d; And as he pluck’d his cursed steel away, Mark how the blood of Caesar follow’d it, As rushing out of doors, to be resolv’d If Brutus so unkindly knock’d, or no; For Brutus, as you know, was Caesar’s angel. Judge, O you gods, how dearly Caesar lov’d him. This was the most unkindest cut of all; For when the noble Caesar saw him stab, Ingratitude, more strong than traitors’ arms, Quite vanquish’d him: then burst his mighty heart; And in his mantle muffling up his face, Even at the base of Pompey’s statue Which all the while ran blood, great Caesar fell. O, what a fall was there, my countrymen! Then I, and you, and all of us fell down, Whilst bloody treason flourish’d over us. O, now you weep; and I perceive you feel The dint of pity. These are gracious drops. Kind souls, what weep you when you but behold Our Caesar’s vesture wounded? Look you here, Here is himself, marr’d, as you see, with traitors.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. O piteous spectacle!
paras.t: O piteous spectacle!

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. O noble Caesar!
paras.t: O noble Caesar!

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. O woeful day!
paras.t: O woeful day!

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. O traitors, villains!
paras.t: O traitors, villains!

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. O most bloody sight!
paras.t: O most bloody sight!

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. We will be revenged.
paras.t: We will be revenged.

paras.html: CITIZENS. Revenge,—about,—seek,—burn,—fire,—kill,—slay,—let not a traitor live!
paras.t: Revenge,—about,—seek,—burn,—fire,—kill,—slay,—let not a traitor live!

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Stay, countrymen.
paras.t: Stay, countrymen.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. Peace there! Hear the noble Antony.
paras.t: Peace there! Hear the noble Antony.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. We’ll hear him, we’ll follow him, we’ll die with him.
paras.t: We’ll hear him, we’ll follow him, we’ll die with him.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Good friends, sweet friends, let me not stir you up
To such a sudden flood of mutiny.
They that have done this deed are honourable.
What private griefs they have, alas, I know not,
That made them do it. They’re wise and honourable,
And will, no doubt, with reasons answer you.
I come not, friends, to steal away your hearts.
I am no orator, as Brutus is;
But, as you know me all, a plain blunt man,
That love my friend; and that they know full well
That gave me public leave to speak of him.
For I have neither wit, nor words, nor worth,
Action, nor utterance, nor the power of speech,
To stir men’s blood. I only speak right on.
I tell you that which you yourselves do know,
Show you sweet Caesar’s wounds, poor poor dumb mouths,
And bid them speak for me. But were I Brutus,
And Brutus Antony, there were an Antony
Would ruffle up your spirits, and put a tongue
In every wound of Caesar, that should move
The stones of Rome to rise and mutiny.
paras.t: Good friends, sweet friends, let me not stir you up To such a sudden flood of mutiny. They that have done this deed are honourable. What private griefs they have, alas, I know not, That made them do it. They’re wise and honourable, And will, no doubt, with reasons answer you. I come not, friends, to steal away your hearts. I am no orator, as Brutus is; But, as you know me all, a plain blunt man, That love my friend; and that they know full well That gave me public leave to speak of him. For I have neither wit, nor words, nor worth, Action, nor utterance, nor the power of speech, To stir men’s blood. I only speak right on. I tell you that which you yourselves do know, Show you sweet Caesar’s wounds, poor poor dumb mouths, And bid them speak for me. But were I Brutus, And Brutus Antony, there were an Antony Would ruffle up your spirits, and put a tongue In every wound of Caesar, that should move The stones of Rome to rise and mutiny.

paras.html: CITIZENS. We’ll mutiny.
paras.t: We’ll mutiny.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. We’ll burn the house of Brutus.
paras.t: We’ll burn the house of Brutus.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. Away, then! come, seek the conspirators.
paras.t: Away, then! come, seek the conspirators.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Yet hear me, countrymen; yet hear me speak.
paras.t: Yet hear me, countrymen; yet hear me speak.

paras.html: CITIZENS. Peace, ho! Hear Antony; most noble Antony.
paras.t: Peace, ho! Hear Antony; most noble Antony.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Why, friends, you go to do you know not what.
Wherein hath Caesar thus deserved your loves?
Alas, you know not; I must tell you then.
You have forgot the will I told you of.
paras.t: Why, friends, you go to do you know not what. Wherein hath Caesar thus deserved your loves? Alas, you know not; I must tell you then. You have forgot the will I told you of.

paras.html: CITIZENS. Most true; the will!—let’s stay, and hear the will.
paras.t: Most true; the will!—let’s stay, and hear the will.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Here is the will, and under Caesar’s seal.
To every Roman citizen he gives,
To every several man, seventy-five drachmas.
paras.t: Here is the will, and under Caesar’s seal. To every Roman citizen he gives, To every several man, seventy-five drachmas.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Most noble Caesar! We’ll revenge his death.
paras.t: Most noble Caesar! We’ll revenge his death.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. O, royal Caesar!
paras.t: O, royal Caesar!

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Hear me with patience.
paras.t: Hear me with patience.

paras.html: CITIZENS. Peace, ho!
paras.t: Peace, ho!

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Moreover, he hath left you all his walks,
His private arbors, and new-planted orchards,
On this side Tiber; he hath left them you,
And to your heirs forever; common pleasures,
To walk abroad, and recreate yourselves.
Here was a Caesar! when comes such another?
paras.t: Moreover, he hath left you all his walks, His private arbors, and new-planted orchards, On this side Tiber; he hath left them you, And to your heirs forever; common pleasures, To walk abroad, and recreate yourselves. Here was a Caesar! when comes such another?

paras.html:
FIRST CITIZEN. Never, never. Come, away, away!
We’ll burn his body in the holy place,
And with the brands fire the traitors’ houses.
Take up the body.
paras.t: Never, never. Come, away, away! We’ll burn his body in the holy place, And with the brands fire the traitors’ houses. Take up the body.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Go, fetch fire.
paras.t: Go, fetch fire.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. Pluck down benches.
paras.t: Pluck down benches.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. Pluck down forms, windows, anything.
paras.t: Pluck down forms, windows, anything.

paras.html: Exeunt Citizens, with the body.
paras.t: Exeunt Citizens, with the body.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Now let it work. Mischief, thou art afoot,
Take thou what course thou wilt!
paras.t: Now let it work. Mischief, thou art afoot, Take thou what course thou wilt!

paras.html: Enter a Servant.
paras.t: Enter a Servant.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. How now, fellow?
paras.t: How now, fellow?

paras.html: SERVANT. Sir, Octavius is already come to Rome.
paras.t: Sir, Octavius is already come to Rome.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Where is he?
paras.t: Where is he?

paras.html: SERVANT. He and Lepidus are at Caesar’s house.
paras.t: He and Lepidus are at Caesar’s house.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. And thither will I straight to visit him.
He comes upon a wish. Fortune is merry,
And in this mood will give us anything.
paras.t: And thither will I straight to visit him. He comes upon a wish. Fortune is merry, And in this mood will give us anything.

paras.html:
SERVANT. I heard him say Brutus and Cassius
Are rid like madmen through the gates of Rome.
paras.t: I heard him say Brutus and Cassius Are rid like madmen through the gates of Rome.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Belike they had some notice of the people,
How I had moved them. Bring me to Octavius.
paras.t: Belike they had some notice of the people, How I had moved them. Bring me to Octavius.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene III · The same. A street

paras.html: Enter Cinna, the poet, and after him the citizens.
paras.t: Enter Cinna, the poet, and after him the citizens.

paras.html:
CINNA THE POET. I dreamt tonight that I did feast with Caesar,
And things unluckily charge my fantasy.
I have no will to wander forth of doors,
Yet something leads me forth.
paras.t: I dreamt tonight that I did feast with Caesar, And things unluckily charge my fantasy. I have no will to wander forth of doors, Yet something leads me forth.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. What is your name?
paras.t: What is your name?

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Whither are you going?
paras.t: Whither are you going?

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. Where do you dwell?
paras.t: Where do you dwell?

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. Are you a married man or a bachelor?
paras.t: Are you a married man or a bachelor?

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. Answer every man directly.
paras.t: Answer every man directly.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. Ay, and briefly.
paras.t: Ay, and briefly.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. Ay, and wisely.
paras.t: Ay, and wisely.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. Ay, and truly, you were best.
paras.t: Ay, and truly, you were best.

paras.html: CINNA THE POET. What is my name? Whither am I going? Where do I dwell? Am I a married man or a bachelor? Then, to answer every man directly and briefly, wisely and truly. Wisely I say I am a bachelor.
paras.t: What is my name? Whither am I going? Where do I dwell? Am I a married man or a bachelor? Then, to answer every man directly and briefly, wisely and truly. Wisely I say I am a bachelor.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. That’s as much as to say they are fools that marry; you’ll bear me a bang for that, I fear. Proceed, directly.
paras.t: That’s as much as to say they are fools that marry; you’ll bear me a bang for that, I fear. Proceed, directly.

paras.html: CINNA THE POET. Directly, I am going to Caesar’s funeral.
paras.t: Directly, I am going to Caesar’s funeral.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. As a friend, or an enemy?
paras.t: As a friend, or an enemy?

paras.html: CINNA THE POET. As a friend.
paras.t: As a friend.

paras.html: SECOND CITIZEN. That matter is answered directly.
paras.t: That matter is answered directly.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. For your dwelling, briefly.
paras.t: For your dwelling, briefly.

paras.html: CINNA THE POET. Briefly, I dwell by the Capitol.
paras.t: Briefly, I dwell by the Capitol.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. Your name, sir, truly.
paras.t: Your name, sir, truly.

paras.html: CINNA THE POET. Truly, my name is Cinna.
paras.t: Truly, my name is Cinna.

paras.html: FIRST CITIZEN. Tear him to pieces! He’s a conspirator.
paras.t: Tear him to pieces! He’s a conspirator.

paras.html: CINNA THE POET. I am Cinna the poet, I am Cinna the poet.
paras.t: I am Cinna the poet, I am Cinna the poet.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. Tear him for his bad verses, tear him for his bad verses.
paras.t: Tear him for his bad verses, tear him for his bad verses.

paras.html: CINNA THE POET. I am not Cinna the conspirator.
paras.t: I am not Cinna the conspirator.

paras.html: FOURTH CITIZEN. It is no matter, his name’s Cinna; pluck but his name out of his heart, and turn him going.
paras.t: It is no matter, his name’s Cinna; pluck but his name out of his heart, and turn him going.

paras.html: THIRD CITIZEN. Tear him, tear him! Come; brands, ho! firebrands. To Brutus’, to Cassius’; burn all. Some to Decius’ house, and some to Casca’s, some to Ligarius’. Away, go!
paras.t: Tear him, tear him! Come; brands, ho! firebrands. To Brutus’, to Cassius’; burn all. Some to Decius’ house, and some to Casca’s, some to Ligarius’. Away, go!

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene I · Rome. A room in Antony’s house

paras.html: Enter Antony, Octavius and Lepidus, seated at a table.
paras.t: Enter Antony, Octavius and Lepidus, seated at a table.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. These many then shall die; their names are prick’d.
paras.t: These many then shall die; their names are prick’d.

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Your brother too must die; consent you, Lepidus?
paras.t: Your brother too must die; consent you, Lepidus?

paras.html: LEPIDUS. I do consent,—
paras.t: I do consent,—

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Prick him down, Antony.
paras.t: Prick him down, Antony.

paras.html:
LEPIDUS. Upon condition Publius shall not live,
Who is your sister’s son, Mark Antony.
paras.t: Upon condition Publius shall not live, Who is your sister’s son, Mark Antony.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him.
But, Lepidus, go you to Caesar’s house;
Fetch the will hither, and we shall determine
How to cut off some charge in legacies.
paras.t: He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him. But, Lepidus, go you to Caesar’s house; Fetch the will hither, and we shall determine How to cut off some charge in legacies.

paras.html: LEPIDUS. What, shall I find you here?
paras.t: What, shall I find you here?

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Or here, or at the Capitol.
paras.t: Or here, or at the Capitol.

paras.html: Exit Lepidus.
paras.t: Exit Lepidus.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. This is a slight unmeritable man,
Meet to be sent on errands. Is it fit,
The three-fold world divided, he should stand
One of the three to share it?
paras.t: This is a slight unmeritable man, Meet to be sent on errands. Is it fit, The three-fold world divided, he should stand One of the three to share it?

paras.html:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR. So you thought him,
And took his voice who should be prick’d to die
In our black sentence and proscription.
paras.t: So you thought him, And took his voice who should be prick’d to die In our black sentence and proscription.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Octavius, I have seen more days than you;
And though we lay these honours on this man,
To ease ourselves of divers sland’rous loads,
He shall but bear them as the ass bears gold,
To groan and sweat under the business,
Either led or driven, as we point the way;
And having brought our treasure where we will,
Then take we down his load, and turn him off,
Like to the empty ass, to shake his ears,
And graze in commons.
paras.t: Octavius, I have seen more days than you; And though we lay these honours on this man, To ease ourselves of divers sland’rous loads, He shall but bear them as the ass bears gold, To groan and sweat under the business, Either led or driven, as we point the way; And having brought our treasure where we will, Then take we down his load, and turn him off, Like to the empty ass, to shake his ears, And graze in commons.

paras.html:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR. You may do your will;
But he’s a tried and valiant soldier.
paras.t: You may do your will; But he’s a tried and valiant soldier.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. So is my horse, Octavius; and for that
I do appoint him store of provender.
It is a creature that I teach to fight,
To wind, to stop, to run directly on,
His corporal motion govern’d by my spirit.
And, in some taste, is Lepidus but so:
He must be taught, and train’d, and bid go forth:
A barren-spirited fellow; one that feeds
On objects, arts, and imitations,
Which, out of use and stal’d by other men,
Begin his fashion. Do not talk of him
But as a property. And now, Octavius,
Listen great things. Brutus and Cassius
Are levying powers; we must straight make head.
Therefore let our alliance be combin’d,
Our best friends made, our means stretch’d;
And let us presently go sit in council,
How covert matters may be best disclos’d,
And open perils surest answered.
paras.t: So is my horse, Octavius; and for that I do appoint him store of provender. It is a creature that I teach to fight, To wind, to stop, to run directly on, His corporal motion govern’d by my spirit. And, in some taste, is Lepidus but so: He must be taught, and train’d, and bid go forth: A barren-spirited fellow; one that feeds On objects, arts, and imitations, Which, out of use and stal’d by other men, Begin his fashion. Do not talk of him But as a property. And now, Octavius, Listen great things. Brutus and Cassius Are levying powers; we must straight make head. Therefore let our alliance be combin’d, Our best friends made, our means stretch’d; And let us presently go sit in council, How covert matters may be best disclos’d, And open perils surest answered.

paras.html:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Let us do so: for we are at the stake,
And bay’d about with many enemies;
And some that smile have in their hearts, I fear,
Millions of mischiefs.
paras.t: Let us do so: for we are at the stake, And bay’d about with many enemies; And some that smile have in their hearts, I fear, Millions of mischiefs.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene II · Before Brutus’ tent, in the camp near Sardis

paras.html: Drum. Enter Brutus, Lucilius, Titinius and Soldiers; Pindarus meeting them; Lucius at some distance.
paras.t: Drum. Enter Brutus, Lucilius, Titinius and Soldiers; Pindarus meeting them; Lucius at some distance.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Stand, ho!
paras.t: Stand, ho!

paras.html: LUCILIUS. Give the word, ho! and stand.
paras.t: Give the word, ho! and stand.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. What now, Lucilius! is Cassius near?
paras.t: What now, Lucilius! is Cassius near?

paras.html:
LUCILIUS. He is at hand, and Pindarus is come
To do you salutation from his master.
paras.t: He is at hand, and Pindarus is come To do you salutation from his master.

paras.html: Pindarus gives a letter to Brutus.
paras.t: Pindarus gives a letter to Brutus.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. He greets me well. Your master, Pindarus,
In his own change, or by ill officers,
Hath given me some worthy cause to wish
Things done, undone: but, if he be at hand,
I shall be satisfied.
paras.t: He greets me well. Your master, Pindarus, In his own change, or by ill officers, Hath given me some worthy cause to wish Things done, undone: but, if he be at hand, I shall be satisfied.

paras.html:
PINDARUS. I do not doubt
But that my noble master will appear
Such as he is, full of regard and honour.
paras.t: I do not doubt But that my noble master will appear Such as he is, full of regard and honour.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. He is not doubted. A word, Lucilius;
How he received you, let me be resolv’d.
paras.t: He is not doubted. A word, Lucilius; How he received you, let me be resolv’d.

paras.html:
LUCILIUS. With courtesy and with respect enough,
But not with such familiar instances,
Nor with such free and friendly conference,
As he hath us’d of old.
paras.t: With courtesy and with respect enough, But not with such familiar instances, Nor with such free and friendly conference, As he hath us’d of old.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Thou hast describ’d
A hot friend cooling. Ever note, Lucilius,
When love begins to sicken and decay
It useth an enforced ceremony.
There are no tricks in plain and simple faith;
But hollow men, like horses hot at hand,
Make gallant show and promise of their mettle;
paras.t: Thou hast describ’d A hot friend cooling. Ever note, Lucilius, When love begins to sicken and decay It useth an enforced ceremony. There are no tricks in plain and simple faith; But hollow men, like horses hot at hand, Make gallant show and promise of their mettle;

paras.html: Low march within.
paras.t: Low march within.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. But when they should endure the bloody spur,
They fall their crests, and like deceitful jades
Sink in the trial. Comes his army on?
paras.t: But when they should endure the bloody spur, They fall their crests, and like deceitful jades Sink in the trial. Comes his army on?

paras.html:
LUCILIUS. They meant this night in Sardis to be quarter’d;
The greater part, the horse in general,
Are come with Cassius.
paras.t: They meant this night in Sardis to be quarter’d; The greater part, the horse in general, Are come with Cassius.

paras.html: Enter Cassius and Soldiers.
paras.t: Enter Cassius and Soldiers.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Hark! he is arriv’d.
March gently on to meet him.
paras.t: Hark! he is arriv’d. March gently on to meet him.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Stand, ho!
paras.t: Stand, ho!

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Stand, ho! Speak the word along.
paras.t: Stand, ho! Speak the word along.

paras.html: FIRST SOLDIER. Stand!
paras.t: Stand!

paras.html: SECOND SOLDIER. Stand!
paras.t: Stand!

paras.html: THIRD SOLDIER. Stand!
paras.t: Stand!

paras.html: CASSIUS. Most noble brother, you have done me wrong.
paras.t: Most noble brother, you have done me wrong.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Judge me, you gods; wrong I mine enemies?
And if not so, how should I wrong a brother?
paras.t: Judge me, you gods; wrong I mine enemies? And if not so, how should I wrong a brother?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Brutus, this sober form of yours hides wrongs;
And when you do them—
paras.t: Brutus, this sober form of yours hides wrongs; And when you do them—

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Cassius, be content.
Speak your griefs softly, I do know you well.
Before the eyes of both our armies here,
Which should perceive nothing but love from us,
Let us not wrangle. Bid them move away;
Then in my tent, Cassius, enlarge your griefs,
And I will give you audience.
paras.t: Cassius, be content. Speak your griefs softly, I do know you well. Before the eyes of both our armies here, Which should perceive nothing but love from us, Let us not wrangle. Bid them move away; Then in my tent, Cassius, enlarge your griefs, And I will give you audience.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Pindarus,
Bid our commanders lead their charges off
A little from this ground.
paras.t: Pindarus, Bid our commanders lead their charges off A little from this ground.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Lucilius, do you the like; and let no man
Come to our tent till we have done our conference.
Lucius and Titinius, guard our door.
paras.t: Lucilius, do you the like; and let no man Come to our tent till we have done our conference. Lucius and Titinius, guard our door.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene III · Within the tent of Brutus

paras.html: Enter Brutus and Cassius.
paras.t: Enter Brutus and Cassius.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. That you have wrong’d me doth appear in this:
You have condemn’d and noted Lucius Pella
For taking bribes here of the Sardians;
Wherein my letters, praying on his side
Because I knew the man, were slighted off.
paras.t: That you have wrong’d me doth appear in this: You have condemn’d and noted Lucius Pella For taking bribes here of the Sardians; Wherein my letters, praying on his side Because I knew the man, were slighted off.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. You wrong’d yourself to write in such a case.
paras.t: You wrong’d yourself to write in such a case.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. In such a time as this it is not meet
That every nice offence should bear his comment.
paras.t: In such a time as this it is not meet That every nice offence should bear his comment.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Let me tell you, Cassius, you yourself
Are much condemn’d to have an itching palm,
To sell and mart your offices for gold
To undeservers.
paras.t: Let me tell you, Cassius, you yourself Are much condemn’d to have an itching palm, To sell and mart your offices for gold To undeservers.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. I an itching palm!
You know that you are Brutus that speak this,
Or, by the gods, this speech were else your last.
paras.t: I an itching palm! You know that you are Brutus that speak this, Or, by the gods, this speech were else your last.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. The name of Cassius honours this corruption,
And chastisement doth therefore hide his head.
paras.t: The name of Cassius honours this corruption, And chastisement doth therefore hide his head.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Chastisement!
paras.t: Chastisement!

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Remember March, the Ides of March remember:
Did not great Julius bleed for justice’ sake?
What villain touch’d his body, that did stab,
And not for justice? What! Shall one of us,
That struck the foremost man of all this world
But for supporting robbers, shall we now
Contaminate our fingers with base bribes,
And sell the mighty space of our large honours
For so much trash as may be grasped thus?
I had rather be a dog, and bay the moon,
Than such a Roman.
paras.t: Remember March, the Ides of March remember: Did not great Julius bleed for justice’ sake? What villain touch’d his body, that did stab, And not for justice? What! Shall one of us, That struck the foremost man of all this world But for supporting robbers, shall we now Contaminate our fingers with base bribes, And sell the mighty space of our large honours For so much trash as may be grasped thus? I had rather be a dog, and bay the moon, Than such a Roman.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Brutus, bait not me,
I’ll not endure it. You forget yourself,
To hedge me in. I am a soldier, I,
Older in practice, abler than yourself
To make conditions.
paras.t: Brutus, bait not me, I’ll not endure it. You forget yourself, To hedge me in. I am a soldier, I, Older in practice, abler than yourself To make conditions.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Go to; you are not, Cassius.
paras.t: Go to; you are not, Cassius.

paras.html: CASSIUS. I am.
paras.t: I am.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. I say you are not.
paras.t: I say you are not.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Urge me no more, I shall forget myself;
Have mind upon your health, tempt me no farther.
paras.t: Urge me no more, I shall forget myself; Have mind upon your health, tempt me no farther.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Away, slight man!
paras.t: Away, slight man!

paras.html: CASSIUS. Is’t possible?
paras.t: Is’t possible?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Hear me, for I will speak.
Must I give way and room to your rash choler?
Shall I be frighted when a madman stares?
paras.t: Hear me, for I will speak. Must I give way and room to your rash choler? Shall I be frighted when a madman stares?

paras.html: CASSIUS. O ye gods, ye gods! Must I endure all this?
paras.t: O ye gods, ye gods! Must I endure all this?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. All this? ay, more: fret till your proud heart break;
Go show your slaves how choleric you are,
And make your bondmen tremble. Must I budge?
Must I observe you? Must I stand and crouch
Under your testy humour? By the gods,
You shall digest the venom of your spleen,
Though it do split you; for, from this day forth,
I’ll use you for my mirth, yea, for my laughter,
When you are waspish.
paras.t: All this? ay, more: fret till your proud heart break; Go show your slaves how choleric you are, And make your bondmen tremble. Must I budge? Must I observe you? Must I stand and crouch Under your testy humour? By the gods, You shall digest the venom of your spleen, Though it do split you; for, from this day forth, I’ll use you for my mirth, yea, for my laughter, When you are waspish.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Is it come to this?
paras.t: Is it come to this?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. You say you are a better soldier:
Let it appear so; make your vaunting true,
And it shall please me well. For mine own part,
I shall be glad to learn of noble men.
paras.t: You say you are a better soldier: Let it appear so; make your vaunting true, And it shall please me well. For mine own part, I shall be glad to learn of noble men.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. You wrong me every way, you wrong me, Brutus.
I said, an elder soldier, not a better:
Did I say better?
paras.t: You wrong me every way, you wrong me, Brutus. I said, an elder soldier, not a better: Did I say better?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. If you did, I care not.
paras.t: If you did, I care not.

paras.html: CASSIUS. When Caesar liv’d, he durst not thus have mov’d me.
paras.t: When Caesar liv’d, he durst not thus have mov’d me.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Peace, peace! you durst not so have tempted him.
paras.t: Peace, peace! you durst not so have tempted him.

paras.html: CASSIUS. I durst not?
paras.t: I durst not?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. No.
paras.t: No.

paras.html: CASSIUS. What? durst not tempt him?
paras.t: What? durst not tempt him?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. For your life you durst not.
paras.t: For your life you durst not.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Do not presume too much upon my love.
I may do that I shall be sorry for.
paras.t: Do not presume too much upon my love. I may do that I shall be sorry for.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. You have done that you should be sorry for.
There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats,
For I am arm’d so strong in honesty,
That they pass by me as the idle wind,
Which I respect not. I did send to you
For certain sums of gold, which you denied me;
For I can raise no money by vile means:
By Heaven, I had rather coin my heart,
And drop my blood for drachmas, than to wring
From the hard hands of peasants their vile trash
By any indirection. I did send
To you for gold to pay my legions,
Which you denied me: was that done like Cassius?
Should I have answer’d Caius Cassius so?
When Marcus Brutus grows so covetous,
To lock such rascal counters from his friends,
Be ready, gods, with all your thunderbolts,
Dash him to pieces!
paras.t: You have done that you should be sorry for. There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats, For I am arm’d so strong in honesty, That they pass by me as the idle wind, Which I respect not. I did send to you For certain sums of gold, which you denied me; For I can raise no money by vile means: By Heaven, I had rather coin my heart, And drop my blood for drachmas, than to wring From the hard hands of peasants their vile trash By any indirection. I did send To you for gold to pay my legions, Which you denied me: was that done like Cassius? Should I have answer’d Caius Cassius so? When Marcus Brutus grows so covetous, To lock such rascal counters from his friends, Be ready, gods, with all your thunderbolts, Dash him to pieces!

paras.html: CASSIUS. I denied you not.
paras.t: I denied you not.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. You did.
paras.t: You did.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. I did not. He was but a fool
That brought my answer back. Brutus hath riv’d my heart.
A friend should bear his friend’s infirmities;
But Brutus makes mine greater than they are.
paras.t: I did not. He was but a fool That brought my answer back. Brutus hath riv’d my heart. A friend should bear his friend’s infirmities; But Brutus makes mine greater than they are.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. I do not, till you practise them on me.
paras.t: I do not, till you practise them on me.

paras.html: CASSIUS. You love me not.
paras.t: You love me not.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. I do not like your faults.
paras.t: I do not like your faults.

paras.html: CASSIUS. A friendly eye could never see such faults.
paras.t: A friendly eye could never see such faults.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. A flatterer’s would not, though they do appear
As huge as high Olympus.
paras.t: A flatterer’s would not, though they do appear As huge as high Olympus.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come,
Revenge yourselves alone on Cassius,
For Cassius is a-weary of the world:
Hated by one he loves; brav’d by his brother;
Check’d like a bondman; all his faults observ’d,
Set in a note-book, learn’d and conn’d by rote,
To cast into my teeth. O, I could weep
My spirit from mine eyes! There is my dagger,
And here my naked breast; within, a heart
Dearer than Plutus’ mine, richer than gold:
If that thou be’st a Roman, take it forth.
I, that denied thee gold, will give my heart:
Strike as thou didst at Caesar; for I know,
When thou didst hate him worst, thou lovedst him better
Than ever thou lovedst Cassius.
paras.t: Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come, Revenge yourselves alone on Cassius, For Cassius is a-weary of the world: Hated by one he loves; brav’d by his brother; Check’d like a bondman; all his faults observ’d, Set in a note-book, learn’d and conn’d by rote, To cast into my teeth. O, I could weep My spirit from mine eyes! There is my dagger, And here my naked breast; within, a heart Dearer than Plutus’ mine, richer than gold: If that thou be’st a Roman, take it forth. I, that denied thee gold, will give my heart: Strike as thou didst at Caesar; for I know, When thou didst hate him worst, thou lovedst him better Than ever thou lovedst Cassius.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Sheathe your dagger.
Be angry when you will, it shall have scope;
Do what you will, dishonour shall be humour.
O Cassius, you are yoked with a lamb
That carries anger as the flint bears fire,
Who, much enforced, shows a hasty spark,
And straight is cold again.
paras.t: Sheathe your dagger. Be angry when you will, it shall have scope; Do what you will, dishonour shall be humour. O Cassius, you are yoked with a lamb That carries anger as the flint bears fire, Who, much enforced, shows a hasty spark, And straight is cold again.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Hath Cassius liv’d
To be but mirth and laughter to his Brutus,
When grief and blood ill-temper’d vexeth him?
paras.t: Hath Cassius liv’d To be but mirth and laughter to his Brutus, When grief and blood ill-temper’d vexeth him?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. When I spoke that, I was ill-temper’d too.
paras.t: When I spoke that, I was ill-temper’d too.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Do you confess so much? Give me your hand.
paras.t: Do you confess so much? Give me your hand.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. And my heart too.
paras.t: And my heart too.

paras.html: CASSIUS. O Brutus!
paras.t: O Brutus!

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. What’s the matter?
paras.t: What’s the matter?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Have not you love enough to bear with me,
When that rash humour which my mother gave me
Makes me forgetful?
paras.t: Have not you love enough to bear with me, When that rash humour which my mother gave me Makes me forgetful?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Yes, Cassius; and from henceforth,
When you are over-earnest with your Brutus,
He’ll think your mother chides, and leave you so.
paras.t: Yes, Cassius; and from henceforth, When you are over-earnest with your Brutus, He’ll think your mother chides, and leave you so.

paras.html: Enter Poet, followed by Lucilius, Titinius and Lucius.
paras.t: Enter Poet, followed by Lucilius, Titinius and Lucius.

paras.html: Within.
paras.t: Within.

paras.html:
A POET. Let me go in to see the generals,
There is some grudge between ’em; ’tis not meet
They be alone.
paras.t: Let me go in to see the generals, There is some grudge between ’em; ’tis not meet They be alone.

paras.html: Within.
paras.t: Within.

paras.html: LUCILIUS. You shall not come to them.
paras.t: You shall not come to them.

paras.html: Within.
paras.t: Within.

paras.html: A POET. Nothing but death shall stay me.
paras.t: Nothing but death shall stay me.

paras.html: CASSIUS. How now! What’s the matter?
paras.t: How now! What’s the matter?

paras.html:
A POET. For shame, you generals! What do you mean?
Love, and be friends, as two such men should be;
For I have seen more years, I’m sure, than ye.
paras.t: For shame, you generals! What do you mean? Love, and be friends, as two such men should be; For I have seen more years, I’m sure, than ye.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Ha, ha! How vilely doth this cynic rhyme!
paras.t: Ha, ha! How vilely doth this cynic rhyme!

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Get you hence, sirrah. Saucy fellow, hence!
paras.t: Get you hence, sirrah. Saucy fellow, hence!

paras.html: CASSIUS. Bear with him, Brutus; ’tis his fashion.
paras.t: Bear with him, Brutus; ’tis his fashion.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. I’ll know his humour when he knows his time.
What should the wars do with these jigging fools?
Companion, hence!
paras.t: I’ll know his humour when he knows his time. What should the wars do with these jigging fools? Companion, hence!

paras.html: CASSIUS. Away, away, be gone!
paras.t: Away, away, be gone!

paras.html: Exit Poet.
paras.t: Exit Poet.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Lucilius and Titinius, bid the commanders
Prepare to lodge their companies tonight.
paras.t: Lucilius and Titinius, bid the commanders Prepare to lodge their companies tonight.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. And come yourselves and bring Messala with you
Immediately to us.
paras.t: And come yourselves and bring Messala with you Immediately to us.

paras.html: Exeunt Lucilius and Titinius.
paras.t: Exeunt Lucilius and Titinius.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Lucius, a bowl of wine.
paras.t: Lucius, a bowl of wine.

paras.html: Exit Lucius.
paras.t: Exit Lucius.

paras.html: CASSIUS. I did not think you could have been so angry.
paras.t: I did not think you could have been so angry.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. O Cassius, I am sick of many griefs.
paras.t: O Cassius, I am sick of many griefs.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Of your philosophy you make no use,
If you give place to accidental evils.
paras.t: Of your philosophy you make no use, If you give place to accidental evils.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. No man bears sorrow better. Portia is dead.
paras.t: No man bears sorrow better. Portia is dead.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Ha? Portia?
paras.t: Ha? Portia?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. She is dead.
paras.t: She is dead.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. How ’scap’d I killing, when I cross’d you so?
O insupportable and touching loss!
Upon what sickness?
paras.t: How ’scap’d I killing, when I cross’d you so? O insupportable and touching loss! Upon what sickness?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Impatient of my absence,
And grief that young Octavius with Mark Antony
Have made themselves so strong; for with her death
That tidings came. With this she fell distract,
And, her attendants absent, swallow’d fire.
paras.t: Impatient of my absence, And grief that young Octavius with Mark Antony Have made themselves so strong; for with her death That tidings came. With this she fell distract, And, her attendants absent, swallow’d fire.

paras.html: CASSIUS. And died so?
paras.t: And died so?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Even so.
paras.t: Even so.

paras.html: CASSIUS. O ye immortal gods!
paras.t: O ye immortal gods!

paras.html: Enter Lucius, with wine and a taper.
paras.t: Enter Lucius, with wine and a taper.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Speak no more of her. Give me a bowl of wine.
In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius.
paras.t: Speak no more of her. Give me a bowl of wine. In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius.

paras.html: Drinks.
paras.t: Drinks.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. My heart is thirsty for that noble pledge.
Fill, Lucius, till the wine o’erswell the cup.
I cannot drink too much of Brutus’ love.
paras.t: My heart is thirsty for that noble pledge. Fill, Lucius, till the wine o’erswell the cup. I cannot drink too much of Brutus’ love.

paras.html: Drinks.
paras.t: Drinks.

paras.html: Exit Lucius.
paras.t: Exit Lucius.

paras.html: Enter Titinius and Messala.
paras.t: Enter Titinius and Messala.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Come in, Titinius!
Welcome, good Messala.
Now sit we close about this taper here,
And call in question our necessities.
paras.t: Come in, Titinius! Welcome, good Messala. Now sit we close about this taper here, And call in question our necessities.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Portia, art thou gone?
paras.t: Portia, art thou gone?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. No more, I pray you.
Messala, I have here received letters,
That young Octavius and Mark Antony
Come down upon us with a mighty power,
Bending their expedition toward Philippi.
paras.t: No more, I pray you. Messala, I have here received letters, That young Octavius and Mark Antony Come down upon us with a mighty power, Bending their expedition toward Philippi.

paras.html: MESSALA. Myself have letters of the selfsame tenor.
paras.t: Myself have letters of the selfsame tenor.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. With what addition?
paras.t: With what addition?

paras.html:
MESSALA. That by proscription and bills of outlawry
Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus
Have put to death an hundred Senators.
paras.t: That by proscription and bills of outlawry Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus Have put to death an hundred Senators.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Therein our letters do not well agree.
Mine speak of seventy Senators that died
By their proscriptions, Cicero being one.
paras.t: Therein our letters do not well agree. Mine speak of seventy Senators that died By their proscriptions, Cicero being one.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Cicero one!
paras.t: Cicero one!

paras.html:
MESSALA. Cicero is dead,
And by that order of proscription.
Had you your letters from your wife, my lord?
paras.t: Cicero is dead, And by that order of proscription. Had you your letters from your wife, my lord?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. No, Messala.
paras.t: No, Messala.

paras.html: MESSALA. Nor nothing in your letters writ of her?
paras.t: Nor nothing in your letters writ of her?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Nothing, Messala.
paras.t: Nothing, Messala.

paras.html: MESSALA. That, methinks, is strange.
paras.t: That, methinks, is strange.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Why ask you? Hear you aught of her in yours?
paras.t: Why ask you? Hear you aught of her in yours?

paras.html: MESSALA. No, my lord.
paras.t: No, my lord.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Now as you are a Roman, tell me true.
paras.t: Now as you are a Roman, tell me true.

paras.html:
MESSALA. Then like a Roman bear the truth I tell,
For certain she is dead, and by strange manner.
paras.t: Then like a Roman bear the truth I tell, For certain she is dead, and by strange manner.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Why, farewell, Portia. We must die, Messala.
With meditating that she must die once,
I have the patience to endure it now.
paras.t: Why, farewell, Portia. We must die, Messala. With meditating that she must die once, I have the patience to endure it now.

paras.html: MESSALA. Even so great men great losses should endure.
paras.t: Even so great men great losses should endure.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. I have as much of this in art as you,
But yet my nature could not bear it so.
paras.t: I have as much of this in art as you, But yet my nature could not bear it so.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Well, to our work alive. What do you think
Of marching to Philippi presently?
paras.t: Well, to our work alive. What do you think Of marching to Philippi presently?

paras.html: CASSIUS. I do not think it good.
paras.t: I do not think it good.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Your reason?
paras.t: Your reason?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. This it is:
’Tis better that the enemy seek us;
So shall he waste his means, weary his soldiers,
Doing himself offence, whilst we, lying still,
Are full of rest, defence, and nimbleness.
paras.t: This it is: ’Tis better that the enemy seek us; So shall he waste his means, weary his soldiers, Doing himself offence, whilst we, lying still, Are full of rest, defence, and nimbleness.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Good reasons must of force give place to better.
The people ’twixt Philippi and this ground
Do stand but in a forced affection;
For they have grudg’d us contribution.
The enemy, marching along by them,
By them shall make a fuller number up,
Come on refresh’d, new-added, and encourag’d;
From which advantage shall we cut him off
If at Philippi we do face him there,
These people at our back.
paras.t: Good reasons must of force give place to better. The people ’twixt Philippi and this ground Do stand but in a forced affection; For they have grudg’d us contribution. The enemy, marching along by them, By them shall make a fuller number up, Come on refresh’d, new-added, and encourag’d; From which advantage shall we cut him off If at Philippi we do face him there, These people at our back.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Hear me, good brother.
paras.t: Hear me, good brother.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Under your pardon. You must note besides,
That we have tried the utmost of our friends,
Our legions are brim-full, our cause is ripe.
The enemy increaseth every day;
We, at the height, are ready to decline.
There is a tide in the affairs of men,
Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune;
Omitted, all the voyage of their life
Is bound in shallows and in miseries.
On such a full sea are we now afloat,
And we must take the current when it serves,
Or lose our ventures.
paras.t: Under your pardon. You must note besides, That we have tried the utmost of our friends, Our legions are brim-full, our cause is ripe. The enemy increaseth every day; We, at the height, are ready to decline. There is a tide in the affairs of men, Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune; Omitted, all the voyage of their life Is bound in shallows and in miseries. On such a full sea are we now afloat, And we must take the current when it serves, Or lose our ventures.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Then, with your will, go on:
We’ll along ourselves, and meet them at Philippi.
paras.t: Then, with your will, go on: We’ll along ourselves, and meet them at Philippi.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. The deep of night is crept upon our talk,
And nature must obey necessity,
Which we will niggard with a little rest.
There is no more to say?
paras.t: The deep of night is crept upon our talk, And nature must obey necessity, Which we will niggard with a little rest. There is no more to say?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. No more. Good night:
Early tomorrow will we rise, and hence.
paras.t: No more. Good night: Early tomorrow will we rise, and hence.

paras.html: Enter Lucius.
paras.t: Enter Lucius.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Lucius! My gown.
paras.t: Lucius! My gown.

paras.html: Exit Lucius.
paras.t: Exit Lucius.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Farewell now, good Messala.
Good night, Titinius. Noble, noble Cassius,
Good night, and good repose.
paras.t: Farewell now, good Messala. Good night, Titinius. Noble, noble Cassius, Good night, and good repose.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. O my dear brother!
This was an ill beginning of the night.
Never come such division ’tween our souls!
Let it not, Brutus.
paras.t: O my dear brother! This was an ill beginning of the night. Never come such division ’tween our souls! Let it not, Brutus.

paras.html: Enter Lucius with the gown.
paras.t: Enter Lucius with the gown.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Everything is well.
paras.t: Everything is well.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Good night, my lord.
paras.t: Good night, my lord.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Good night, good brother.
TITINIUS and MESSALA.
Good night, Lord Brutus.
paras.t: Good night, good brother. TITINIUS and MESSALA. Good night, Lord Brutus.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Farewell, everyone.
paras.t: Farewell, everyone.

paras.html: Exeunt Cassius, Titinius and Messala.
paras.t: Exeunt Cassius, Titinius and Messala.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Give me the gown. Where is thy instrument?
paras.t: Give me the gown. Where is thy instrument?

paras.html: LUCIUS. Here in the tent.
paras.t: Here in the tent.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. What, thou speak’st drowsily?
Poor knave, I blame thee not, thou art o’er-watch’d.
Call Claudius and some other of my men;
I’ll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.
paras.t: What, thou speak’st drowsily? Poor knave, I blame thee not, thou art o’er-watch’d. Call Claudius and some other of my men; I’ll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.

paras.html: LUCIUS. Varro and Claudius!
paras.t: Varro and Claudius!

paras.html: Enter Varro and Claudius.
paras.t: Enter Varro and Claudius.

paras.html: VARRO. Calls my lord?
paras.t: Calls my lord?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. I pray you, sirs, lie in my tent and sleep;
It may be I shall raise you by-and-by
On business to my brother Cassius.
paras.t: I pray you, sirs, lie in my tent and sleep; It may be I shall raise you by-and-by On business to my brother Cassius.

paras.html: VARRO. So please you, we will stand and watch your pleasure.
paras.t: So please you, we will stand and watch your pleasure.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. I will not have it so; lie down, good sirs,
It may be I shall otherwise bethink me.
Look, Lucius, here’s the book I sought for so;
I put it in the pocket of my gown.
paras.t: I will not have it so; lie down, good sirs, It may be I shall otherwise bethink me. Look, Lucius, here’s the book I sought for so; I put it in the pocket of my gown.

paras.html: Servants lie down.
paras.t: Servants lie down.

paras.html: LUCIUS. I was sure your lordship did not give it me.
paras.t: I was sure your lordship did not give it me.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Bear with me, good boy, I am much forgetful.
Canst thou hold up thy heavy eyes awhile,
And touch thy instrument a strain or two?
paras.t: Bear with me, good boy, I am much forgetful. Canst thou hold up thy heavy eyes awhile, And touch thy instrument a strain or two?

paras.html: LUCIUS. Ay, my lord, an’t please you.
paras.t: Ay, my lord, an’t please you.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. It does, my boy.
I trouble thee too much, but thou art willing.
paras.t: It does, my boy. I trouble thee too much, but thou art willing.

paras.html: LUCIUS. It is my duty, sir.
paras.t: It is my duty, sir.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. I should not urge thy duty past thy might;
I know young bloods look for a time of rest.
paras.t: I should not urge thy duty past thy might; I know young bloods look for a time of rest.

paras.html: LUCIUS. I have slept, my lord, already.
paras.t: I have slept, my lord, already.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. It was well done, and thou shalt sleep again;
I will not hold thee long. If I do live,
I will be good to thee.
paras.t: It was well done, and thou shalt sleep again; I will not hold thee long. If I do live, I will be good to thee.

paras.html: Lucius plays and sings till he falls asleep.
paras.t: Lucius plays and sings till he falls asleep.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. This is a sleepy tune. O murd’rous slumber,
Layest thou thy leaden mace upon my boy,
That plays thee music? Gentle knave, good night;
I will not do thee so much wrong to wake thee.
If thou dost nod, thou break’st thy instrument;
I’ll take it from thee; and, good boy, good night.
Let me see, let me see; is not the leaf turn’d down
Where I left reading? Here it is, I think.
paras.t: This is a sleepy tune. O murd’rous slumber, Layest thou thy leaden mace upon my boy, That plays thee music? Gentle knave, good night; I will not do thee so much wrong to wake thee. If thou dost nod, thou break’st thy instrument; I’ll take it from thee; and, good boy, good night. Let me see, let me see; is not the leaf turn’d down Where I left reading? Here it is, I think.

paras.html: Enter the Ghost of Caesar.
paras.t: Enter the Ghost of Caesar.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. How ill this taper burns! Ha! who comes here?
I think it is the weakness of mine eyes
That shapes this monstrous apparition.
It comes upon me. Art thou anything?
Art thou some god, some angel, or some devil,
That mak’st my blood cold and my hair to stare?
Speak to me what thou art.
paras.t: How ill this taper burns! Ha! who comes here? I think it is the weakness of mine eyes That shapes this monstrous apparition. It comes upon me. Art thou anything? Art thou some god, some angel, or some devil, That mak’st my blood cold and my hair to stare? Speak to me what thou art.

paras.html: GHOST OF CAESAR. Thy evil spirit, Brutus.
paras.t: Thy evil spirit, Brutus.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Why com’st thou?
paras.t: Why com’st thou?

paras.html: GHOST OF CAESAR. To tell thee thou shalt see me at Philippi.
paras.t: To tell thee thou shalt see me at Philippi.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Well; then I shall see thee again?
paras.t: Well; then I shall see thee again?

paras.html: GHOST OF CAESAR. Ay, at Philippi.
paras.t: Ay, at Philippi.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Why, I will see thee at Philippi then.
paras.t: Why, I will see thee at Philippi then.

paras.html: Ghost vanishes.
paras.t: Ghost vanishes.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Now I have taken heart, thou vanishest.
Ill spirit, I would hold more talk with thee.
Boy! Lucius! Varro! Claudius! Sirs, awake! Claudius!
paras.t: Now I have taken heart, thou vanishest. Ill spirit, I would hold more talk with thee. Boy! Lucius! Varro! Claudius! Sirs, awake! Claudius!

paras.html: LUCIUS. The strings, my lord, are false.
paras.t: The strings, my lord, are false.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. He thinks he still is at his instrument.
Lucius, awake!
paras.t: He thinks he still is at his instrument. Lucius, awake!

paras.html: LUCIUS. My lord?
paras.t: My lord?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Didst thou dream, Lucius, that thou so criedst out?
paras.t: Didst thou dream, Lucius, that thou so criedst out?

paras.html: LUCIUS. My lord, I do not know that I did cry.
paras.t: My lord, I do not know that I did cry.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Yes, that thou didst. Didst thou see anything?
paras.t: Yes, that thou didst. Didst thou see anything?

paras.html: LUCIUS. Nothing, my lord.
paras.t: Nothing, my lord.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Sleep again, Lucius. Sirrah Claudius!
Fellow thou, awake!
paras.t: Sleep again, Lucius. Sirrah Claudius! Fellow thou, awake!

paras.html: VARRO. My lord?
paras.t: My lord?

paras.html: CLAUDIUS. My lord?
paras.t: My lord?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Why did you so cry out, sirs, in your sleep?
paras.t: Why did you so cry out, sirs, in your sleep?

paras.html: VARRO. Did we, my lord?
paras.t: Did we, my lord?

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Ay. Saw you anything?
paras.t: Ay. Saw you anything?

paras.html: VARRO. No, my lord, I saw nothing.
paras.t: No, my lord, I saw nothing.

paras.html: CLAUDIUS. Nor I, my lord.
paras.t: Nor I, my lord.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Go and commend me to my brother Cassius;
Bid him set on his powers betimes before,
And we will follow.
paras.t: Go and commend me to my brother Cassius; Bid him set on his powers betimes before, And we will follow.

paras.html: VARRO. It shall be done, my lord.
paras.t: It shall be done, my lord.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene I · The plains of Philippi

paras.html: Enter Octavius, Antony and their Army.
paras.t: Enter Octavius, Antony and their Army.

paras.html:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Now, Antony, our hopes are answered.
You said the enemy would not come down,
But keep the hills and upper regions.
It proves not so; their battles are at hand,
They mean to warn us at Philippi here,
Answering before we do demand of them.
paras.t: Now, Antony, our hopes are answered. You said the enemy would not come down, But keep the hills and upper regions. It proves not so; their battles are at hand, They mean to warn us at Philippi here, Answering before we do demand of them.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Tut, I am in their bosoms, and I know
Wherefore they do it. They could be content
To visit other places, and come down
With fearful bravery, thinking by this face
To fasten in our thoughts that they have courage;
But ’tis not so.
paras.t: Tut, I am in their bosoms, and I know Wherefore they do it. They could be content To visit other places, and come down With fearful bravery, thinking by this face To fasten in our thoughts that they have courage; But ’tis not so.

paras.html: Enter a Messenger.
paras.t: Enter a Messenger.

paras.html:
MESSENGER. Prepare you, generals.
The enemy comes on in gallant show;
Their bloody sign of battle is hung out,
And something to be done immediately.
paras.t: Prepare you, generals. The enemy comes on in gallant show; Their bloody sign of battle is hung out, And something to be done immediately.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Octavius, lead your battle softly on
Upon the left hand of the even field.
paras.t: Octavius, lead your battle softly on Upon the left hand of the even field.

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Upon the right hand I. Keep thou the left.
paras.t: Upon the right hand I. Keep thou the left.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Why do you cross me in this exigent?
paras.t: Why do you cross me in this exigent?

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. I do not cross you; but I will do so.
paras.t: I do not cross you; but I will do so.

paras.html: March.
paras.t: March.

paras.html: Drum. Enter Brutus, Cassius and their Army; Lucilius, Titinius, Messala and others.
paras.t: Drum. Enter Brutus, Cassius and their Army; Lucilius, Titinius, Messala and others.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. They stand, and would have parley.
paras.t: They stand, and would have parley.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Stand fast, Titinius; we must out and talk.
paras.t: Stand fast, Titinius; we must out and talk.

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Mark Antony, shall we give sign of battle?
paras.t: Mark Antony, shall we give sign of battle?

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. No, Caesar, we will answer on their charge.
Make forth; the generals would have some words.
paras.t: No, Caesar, we will answer on their charge. Make forth; the generals would have some words.

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Stir not until the signal.
paras.t: Stir not until the signal.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Words before blows: is it so, countrymen?
paras.t: Words before blows: is it so, countrymen?

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Not that we love words better, as you do.
paras.t: Not that we love words better, as you do.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Good words are better than bad strokes, Octavius.
paras.t: Good words are better than bad strokes, Octavius.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. In your bad strokes, Brutus, you give good words;
Witness the hole you made in Caesar’s heart,
Crying, “Long live! Hail, Caesar!”
paras.t: In your bad strokes, Brutus, you give good words; Witness the hole you made in Caesar’s heart, Crying, “Long live! Hail, Caesar!”

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Antony,
The posture of your blows are yet unknown;
But for your words, they rob the Hybla bees,
And leave them honeyless.
paras.t: Antony, The posture of your blows are yet unknown; But for your words, they rob the Hybla bees, And leave them honeyless.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Not stingless too.
paras.t: Not stingless too.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. O yes, and soundless too,
For you have stol’n their buzzing, Antony,
And very wisely threat before you sting.
paras.t: O yes, and soundless too, For you have stol’n their buzzing, Antony, And very wisely threat before you sting.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. Villains, you did not so when your vile daggers
Hack’d one another in the sides of Caesar:
You show’d your teeth like apes, and fawn’d like hounds,
And bow’d like bondmen, kissing Caesar’s feet;
Whilst damned Casca, like a cur, behind
Struck Caesar on the neck. O you flatterers!
paras.t: Villains, you did not so when your vile daggers Hack’d one another in the sides of Caesar: You show’d your teeth like apes, and fawn’d like hounds, And bow’d like bondmen, kissing Caesar’s feet; Whilst damned Casca, like a cur, behind Struck Caesar on the neck. O you flatterers!

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Flatterers! Now, Brutus, thank yourself.
This tongue had not offended so today,
If Cassius might have rul’d.
paras.t: Flatterers! Now, Brutus, thank yourself. This tongue had not offended so today, If Cassius might have rul’d.

paras.html:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Come, come, the cause. If arguing makes us sweat,
The proof of it will turn to redder drops.
Look, I draw a sword against conspirators.
When think you that the sword goes up again?
Never, till Caesar’s three and thirty wounds
Be well aveng’d; or till another Caesar
Have added slaughter to the sword of traitors.
paras.t: Come, come, the cause. If arguing makes us sweat, The proof of it will turn to redder drops. Look, I draw a sword against conspirators. When think you that the sword goes up again? Never, till Caesar’s three and thirty wounds Be well aveng’d; or till another Caesar Have added slaughter to the sword of traitors.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Caesar, thou canst not die by traitors’ hands,
Unless thou bring’st them with thee.
paras.t: Caesar, thou canst not die by traitors’ hands, Unless thou bring’st them with thee.

paras.html:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR. So I hope.
I was not born to die on Brutus’ sword.
paras.t: So I hope. I was not born to die on Brutus’ sword.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. O, if thou wert the noblest of thy strain,
Young man, thou couldst not die more honourable.
paras.t: O, if thou wert the noblest of thy strain, Young man, thou couldst not die more honourable.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. A peevish school-boy, worthless of such honour,
Join’d with a masker and a reveller.
paras.t: A peevish school-boy, worthless of such honour, Join’d with a masker and a reveller.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Old Cassius still!
paras.t: Old Cassius still!

paras.html:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Come, Antony; away!
Defiance, traitors, hurl we in your teeth.
If you dare fight today, come to the field;
If not, when you have stomachs.
paras.t: Come, Antony; away! Defiance, traitors, hurl we in your teeth. If you dare fight today, come to the field; If not, when you have stomachs.

paras.html: Exeunt Octavius, Antony and their Army.
paras.t: Exeunt Octavius, Antony and their Army.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Why now, blow wind, swell billow, and swim bark!
The storm is up, and all is on the hazard.
paras.t: Why now, blow wind, swell billow, and swim bark! The storm is up, and all is on the hazard.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Ho, Lucilius! Hark, a word with you.
paras.t: Ho, Lucilius! Hark, a word with you.

paras.html: LUCILIUS. My lord?
paras.t: My lord?

paras.html: Brutus and Lucilius talk apart.
paras.t: Brutus and Lucilius talk apart.

paras.html: CASSIUS. Messala.
paras.t: Messala.

paras.html: MESSALA. What says my General?
paras.t: What says my General?

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Messala,
This is my birth-day; as this very day
Was Cassius born. Give me thy hand, Messala:
Be thou my witness that against my will
As Pompey was, am I compell’d to set
Upon one battle all our liberties.
You know that I held Epicurus strong,
And his opinion. Now I change my mind,
And partly credit things that do presage.
Coming from Sardis, on our former ensign
Two mighty eagles fell, and there they perch’d,
Gorging and feeding from our soldiers’ hands,
Who to Philippi here consorted us.
This morning are they fled away and gone,
And in their steads do ravens, crows, and kites
Fly o’er our heads, and downward look on us,
As we were sickly prey: their shadows seem
A canopy most fatal, under which
Our army lies, ready to give up the ghost.
paras.t: Messala, This is my birth-day; as this very day Was Cassius born. Give me thy hand, Messala: Be thou my witness that against my will As Pompey was, am I compell’d to set Upon one battle all our liberties. You know that I held Epicurus strong, And his opinion. Now I change my mind, And partly credit things that do presage. Coming from Sardis, on our former ensign Two mighty eagles fell, and there they perch’d, Gorging and feeding from our soldiers’ hands, Who to Philippi here consorted us. This morning are they fled away and gone, And in their steads do ravens, crows, and kites Fly o’er our heads, and downward look on us, As we were sickly prey: their shadows seem A canopy most fatal, under which Our army lies, ready to give up the ghost.

paras.html: MESSALA. Believe not so.
paras.t: Believe not so.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. I but believe it partly,
For I am fresh of spirit, and resolv’d
To meet all perils very constantly.
paras.t: I but believe it partly, For I am fresh of spirit, and resolv’d To meet all perils very constantly.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Even so, Lucilius.
paras.t: Even so, Lucilius.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Now, most noble Brutus,
The gods today stand friendly, that we may,
Lovers in peace, lead on our days to age!
But, since the affairs of men rest still incertain,
Let’s reason with the worst that may befall.
If we do lose this battle, then is this
The very last time we shall speak together:
What are you then determined to do?
paras.t: Now, most noble Brutus, The gods today stand friendly, that we may, Lovers in peace, lead on our days to age! But, since the affairs of men rest still incertain, Let’s reason with the worst that may befall. If we do lose this battle, then is this The very last time we shall speak together: What are you then determined to do?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Even by the rule of that philosophy
By which I did blame Cato for the death
Which he did give himself, I know not how,
But I do find it cowardly and vile,
For fear of what might fall, so to prevent
The time of life, arming myself with patience
To stay the providence of some high powers
That govern us below.
paras.t: Even by the rule of that philosophy By which I did blame Cato for the death Which he did give himself, I know not how, But I do find it cowardly and vile, For fear of what might fall, so to prevent The time of life, arming myself with patience To stay the providence of some high powers That govern us below.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Then, if we lose this battle,
You are contented to be led in triumph
Thorough the streets of Rome?
paras.t: Then, if we lose this battle, You are contented to be led in triumph Thorough the streets of Rome?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. No, Cassius, no: think not, thou noble Roman,
That ever Brutus will go bound to Rome;
He bears too great a mind. But this same day
Must end that work the Ides of March begun;
And whether we shall meet again I know not.
Therefore our everlasting farewell take.
For ever, and for ever, farewell, Cassius.
If we do meet again, why, we shall smile;
If not, why then this parting was well made.
paras.t: No, Cassius, no: think not, thou noble Roman, That ever Brutus will go bound to Rome; He bears too great a mind. But this same day Must end that work the Ides of March begun; And whether we shall meet again I know not. Therefore our everlasting farewell take. For ever, and for ever, farewell, Cassius. If we do meet again, why, we shall smile; If not, why then this parting was well made.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. For ever and for ever farewell, Brutus.
If we do meet again, we’ll smile indeed;
If not, ’tis true this parting was well made.
paras.t: For ever and for ever farewell, Brutus. If we do meet again, we’ll smile indeed; If not, ’tis true this parting was well made.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Why then, lead on. O, that a man might know
The end of this day’s business ere it come!
But it sufficeth that the day will end,
And then the end is known. Come, ho! away!
paras.t: Why then, lead on. O, that a man might know The end of this day’s business ere it come! But it sufficeth that the day will end, And then the end is known. Come, ho! away!

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene II · The same. The field of battle

paras.html: Alarum. Enter Brutus and Messala.
paras.t: Alarum. Enter Brutus and Messala.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Ride, ride, Messala, ride, and give these bills
Unto the legions on the other side.
paras.t: Ride, ride, Messala, ride, and give these bills Unto the legions on the other side.

paras.html: Loud alarum.
paras.t: Loud alarum.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Let them set on at once; for I perceive
But cold demeanor in Octavius’ wing,
And sudden push gives them the overthrow.
Ride, ride, Messala; let them all come down.
paras.t: Let them set on at once; for I perceive But cold demeanor in Octavius’ wing, And sudden push gives them the overthrow. Ride, ride, Messala; let them all come down.
