paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene III · Another part of the field

paras.html: Alarum. Enter Cassius and Titinius.
paras.t: Alarum. Enter Cassius and Titinius.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. O, look, Titinius, look, the villains fly!
Myself have to mine own turn’d enemy:
This ensign here of mine was turning back;
I slew the coward, and did take it from him.
paras.t: O, look, Titinius, look, the villains fly! Myself have to mine own turn’d enemy: This ensign here of mine was turning back; I slew the coward, and did take it from him.

paras.html:
TITINIUS. O Cassius, Brutus gave the word too early,
Who, having some advantage on Octavius,
Took it too eagerly: his soldiers fell to spoil,
Whilst we by Antony are all enclos’d.
paras.t: O Cassius, Brutus gave the word too early, Who, having some advantage on Octavius, Took it too eagerly: his soldiers fell to spoil, Whilst we by Antony are all enclos’d.

paras.html: Enter Pindarus.
paras.t: Enter Pindarus.

paras.html:
PINDARUS. Fly further off, my lord, fly further off;
Mark Antony is in your tents, my lord.
Fly, therefore, noble Cassius, fly far off.
paras.t: Fly further off, my lord, fly further off; Mark Antony is in your tents, my lord. Fly, therefore, noble Cassius, fly far off.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. This hill is far enough. Look, look, Titinius;
Are those my tents where I perceive the fire?
paras.t: This hill is far enough. Look, look, Titinius; Are those my tents where I perceive the fire?

paras.html: TITINIUS. They are, my lord.
paras.t: They are, my lord.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Titinius, if thou lovest me,
Mount thou my horse and hide thy spurs in him,
Till he have brought thee up to yonder troops
And here again, that I may rest assur’d
Whether yond troops are friend or enemy.
paras.t: Titinius, if thou lovest me, Mount thou my horse and hide thy spurs in him, Till he have brought thee up to yonder troops And here again, that I may rest assur’d Whether yond troops are friend or enemy.

paras.html: TITINIUS. I will be here again, even with a thought.
paras.t: I will be here again, even with a thought.

paras.html: Exit.
paras.t: Exit.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Go, Pindarus, get higher on that hill,
My sight was ever thick. Regard Titinius,
And tell me what thou notest about the field.
paras.t: Go, Pindarus, get higher on that hill, My sight was ever thick. Regard Titinius, And tell me what thou notest about the field.

paras.html: Pindarus goes up.
paras.t: Pindarus goes up.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. This day I breathed first. Time is come round,
And where I did begin, there shall I end.
My life is run his compass. Sirrah, what news?
paras.t: This day I breathed first. Time is come round, And where I did begin, there shall I end. My life is run his compass. Sirrah, what news?

paras.html: Above.
paras.t: Above.

paras.html: PINDARUS. O my lord!
paras.t: O my lord!

paras.html: CASSIUS. What news?
paras.t: What news?

paras.html: Above.
paras.t: Above.

paras.html:
PINDARUS. Titinius is enclosed round about
With horsemen, that make to him on the spur,
Yet he spurs on. Now they are almost on him.
Now, Titinius! Now some light. O, he lights too.
He’s ta’en!
paras.t: Titinius is enclosed round about With horsemen, that make to him on the spur, Yet he spurs on. Now they are almost on him. Now, Titinius! Now some light. O, he lights too. He’s ta’en!

paras.html: Shout.
paras.t: Shout.

paras.html: PINDARUS. And, hark! they shout for joy.
paras.t: And, hark! they shout for joy.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Come down; behold no more.
O, coward that I am, to live so long,
To see my best friend ta’en before my face!
paras.t: Come down; behold no more. O, coward that I am, to live so long, To see my best friend ta’en before my face!

paras.html: Pindarus descends.
paras.t: Pindarus descends.

paras.html:
CASSIUS. Come hither, sirrah.
In Parthia did I take thee prisoner;
And then I swore thee, saving of thy life,
That whatsoever I did bid thee do,
Thou shouldst attempt it. Come now, keep thine oath.
Now be a freeman; and with this good sword,
That ran through Caesar’s bowels, search this bosom.
Stand not to answer. Here, take thou the hilts;
And when my face is cover’d, as ’tis now,
Guide thou the sword.—Caesar, thou art reveng’d,
Even with the sword that kill’d thee.
paras.t: Come hither, sirrah. In Parthia did I take thee prisoner; And then I swore thee, saving of thy life, That whatsoever I did bid thee do, Thou shouldst attempt it. Come now, keep thine oath. Now be a freeman; and with this good sword, That ran through Caesar’s bowels, search this bosom. Stand not to answer. Here, take thou the hilts; And when my face is cover’d, as ’tis now, Guide thou the sword.—Caesar, thou art reveng’d, Even with the sword that kill’d thee.

paras.html: Dies.
paras.t: Dies.

paras.html:
PINDARUS. So, I am free, yet would not so have been,
Durst I have done my will. O Cassius!
Far from this country Pindarus shall run,
Where never Roman shall take note of him.
paras.t: So, I am free, yet would not so have been, Durst I have done my will. O Cassius! Far from this country Pindarus shall run, Where never Roman shall take note of him.

paras.html: Exit.
paras.t: Exit.

paras.html: Enter Titinius with Messala.
paras.t: Enter Titinius with Messala.

paras.html:
MESSALA. It is but change, Titinius; for Octavius
Is overthrown by noble Brutus’ power,
As Cassius’ legions are by Antony.
paras.t: It is but change, Titinius; for Octavius Is overthrown by noble Brutus’ power, As Cassius’ legions are by Antony.

paras.html: TITINIUS. These tidings would well comfort Cassius.
paras.t: These tidings would well comfort Cassius.

paras.html: MESSALA. Where did you leave him?
paras.t: Where did you leave him?

paras.html:
TITINIUS. All disconsolate,
With Pindarus his bondman, on this hill.
paras.t: All disconsolate, With Pindarus his bondman, on this hill.

paras.html: MESSALA. Is not that he that lies upon the ground?
paras.t: Is not that he that lies upon the ground?

paras.html: TITINIUS. He lies not like the living. O my heart!
paras.t: He lies not like the living. O my heart!

paras.html: MESSALA. Is not that he?
paras.t: Is not that he?

paras.html:
TITINIUS. No, this was he, Messala,
But Cassius is no more. O setting sun,
As in thy red rays thou dost sink to night,
So in his red blood Cassius’ day is set.
The sun of Rome is set. Our day is gone;
Clouds, dews, and dangers come; our deeds are done.
Mistrust of my success hath done this deed.
paras.t: No, this was he, Messala, But Cassius is no more. O setting sun, As in thy red rays thou dost sink to night, So in his red blood Cassius’ day is set. The sun of Rome is set. Our day is gone; Clouds, dews, and dangers come; our deeds are done. Mistrust of my success hath done this deed.

paras.html:
MESSALA. Mistrust of good success hath done this deed.
O hateful Error, Melancholy’s child!
Why dost thou show to the apt thoughts of men
The things that are not? O Error, soon conceiv’d,
Thou never com’st unto a happy birth,
But kill’st the mother that engender’d thee!
paras.t: Mistrust of good success hath done this deed. O hateful Error, Melancholy’s child! Why dost thou show to the apt thoughts of men The things that are not? O Error, soon conceiv’d, Thou never com’st unto a happy birth, But kill’st the mother that engender’d thee!

paras.html: TITINIUS. What, Pindarus! where art thou, Pindarus?
paras.t: What, Pindarus! where art thou, Pindarus?

paras.html:
MESSALA. Seek him, Titinius, whilst I go to meet
The noble Brutus, thrusting this report
Into his ears. I may say thrusting it;
For piercing steel and darts envenomed
Shall be as welcome to the ears of Brutus
As tidings of this sight.
paras.t: Seek him, Titinius, whilst I go to meet The noble Brutus, thrusting this report Into his ears. I may say thrusting it; For piercing steel and darts envenomed Shall be as welcome to the ears of Brutus As tidings of this sight.

paras.html:
TITINIUS. Hie you, Messala,
And I will seek for Pindarus the while.
paras.t: Hie you, Messala, And I will seek for Pindarus the while.

paras.html: Exit Messala.
paras.t: Exit Messala.

paras.html:
TITINIUS. Why didst thou send me forth, brave Cassius?
Did I not meet thy friends? And did not they
Put on my brows this wreath of victory,
And bid me give it thee? Didst thou not hear their shouts?
Alas, thou hast misconstrued everything!
But, hold thee, take this garland on thy brow;
Thy Brutus bid me give it thee, and I
Will do his bidding. Brutus, come apace,
And see how I regarded Caius Cassius.
By your leave, gods. This is a Roman’s part.
Come, Cassius’ sword, and find Titinius’ heart.
paras.t: Why didst thou send me forth, brave Cassius? Did I not meet thy friends? And did not they Put on my brows this wreath of victory, And bid me give it thee? Didst thou not hear their shouts? Alas, thou hast misconstrued everything! But, hold thee, take this garland on thy brow; Thy Brutus bid me give it thee, and I Will do his bidding. Brutus, come apace, And see how I regarded Caius Cassius. By your leave, gods. This is a Roman’s part. Come, Cassius’ sword, and find Titinius’ heart.

paras.html: Dies.
paras.t: Dies.

paras.html: Alarum. Enter Brutus, Messala, young Cato, Strato, Volumnius and Lucilius.
paras.t: Alarum. Enter Brutus, Messala, young Cato, Strato, Volumnius and Lucilius.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Where, where, Messala, doth his body lie?
paras.t: Where, where, Messala, doth his body lie?

paras.html: MESSALA. Lo, yonder, and Titinius mourning it.
paras.t: Lo, yonder, and Titinius mourning it.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Titinius’ face is upward.
paras.t: Titinius’ face is upward.

paras.html: YOUNG CATO. He is slain.
paras.t: He is slain.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. O Julius Caesar, thou art mighty yet!
Thy spirit walks abroad, and turns our swords
In our own proper entrails.
paras.t: O Julius Caesar, thou art mighty yet! Thy spirit walks abroad, and turns our swords In our own proper entrails.

paras.html: Low alarums.
paras.t: Low alarums.

paras.html:
YOUNG CATO. Brave Titinius!
Look whether he have not crown’d dead Cassius!
paras.t: Brave Titinius! Look whether he have not crown’d dead Cassius!

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Are yet two Romans living such as these?
The last of all the Romans, fare thee well!
It is impossible that ever Rome
Should breed thy fellow. Friends, I owe more tears
To this dead man than you shall see me pay.
I shall find time, Cassius, I shall find time.
Come therefore, and to Thassos send his body.
His funerals shall not be in our camp,
Lest it discomfort us. Lucilius, come;
And come, young Cato; let us to the field.
Labeo and Flavius, set our battles on.
’Tis three o’clock; and Romans, yet ere night
We shall try fortune in a second fight.
paras.t: Are yet two Romans living such as these? The last of all the Romans, fare thee well! It is impossible that ever Rome Should breed thy fellow. Friends, I owe more tears To this dead man than you shall see me pay. I shall find time, Cassius, I shall find time. Come therefore, and to Thassos send his body. His funerals shall not be in our camp, Lest it discomfort us. Lucilius, come; And come, young Cato; let us to the field. Labeo and Flavius, set our battles on. ’Tis three o’clock; and Romans, yet ere night We shall try fortune in a second fight.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene IV · Another part of the field

paras.html: Alarum. Enter fighting soldiers of both armies; then Brutus, Messala, young Cato, Lucilius, Flavius and others.
paras.t: Alarum. Enter fighting soldiers of both armies; then Brutus, Messala, young Cato, Lucilius, Flavius and others.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Yet, countrymen, O, yet hold up your heads!
paras.t: Yet, countrymen, O, yet hold up your heads!

paras.html:
YOUNG CATO. What bastard doth not? Who will go with me?
I will proclaim my name about the field.
I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!
A foe to tyrants, and my country’s friend.
I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!
paras.t: What bastard doth not? Who will go with me? I will proclaim my name about the field. I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho! A foe to tyrants, and my country’s friend. I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!

paras.html: Charges the enemy.
paras.t: Charges the enemy.

paras.html:
LUCILIUS. And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I;
Brutus, my country’s friend; know me for Brutus!
paras.t: And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I; Brutus, my country’s friend; know me for Brutus!

paras.html: Exit, charging the enemy. Cato is overpowered, and falls.
paras.t: Exit, charging the enemy. Cato is overpowered, and falls.

paras.html:
LUCILIUS. O young and noble Cato, art thou down?
Why, now thou diest as bravely as Titinius,
And mayst be honour’d, being Cato’s son.
paras.t: O young and noble Cato, art thou down? Why, now thou diest as bravely as Titinius, And mayst be honour’d, being Cato’s son.

paras.html: FIRST SOLDIER. Yield, or thou diest.
paras.t: Yield, or thou diest.

paras.html:
LUCILIUS. Only I yield to die:
There is so much that thou wilt kill me straight;
paras.t: Only I yield to die: There is so much that thou wilt kill me straight;

paras.html: Offering money
paras.t: Offering money

paras.html: LUCILIUS. Kill Brutus, and be honour’d in his death.
paras.t: Kill Brutus, and be honour’d in his death.

paras.html: FIRST SOLDIER. We must not. A noble prisoner!
paras.t: We must not. A noble prisoner!

paras.html: SECOND SOLDIER. Room, ho! Tell Antony, Brutus is ta’en.
paras.t: Room, ho! Tell Antony, Brutus is ta’en.

paras.html: FIRST SOLDIER. I’ll tell the news. Here comes the General.
paras.t: I’ll tell the news. Here comes the General.

paras.html: Enter Antony.
paras.t: Enter Antony.

paras.html: FIRST SOLDIER. Brutus is ta’en, Brutus is ta’en, my lord.
paras.t: Brutus is ta’en, Brutus is ta’en, my lord.

paras.html: MARK ANTONY. Where is he?
paras.t: Where is he?

paras.html:
LUCILIUS. Safe, Antony; Brutus is safe enough.
I dare assure thee that no enemy
Shall ever take alive the noble Brutus.
The gods defend him from so great a shame!
When you do find him, or alive or dead,
He will be found like Brutus, like himself.
paras.t: Safe, Antony; Brutus is safe enough. I dare assure thee that no enemy Shall ever take alive the noble Brutus. The gods defend him from so great a shame! When you do find him, or alive or dead, He will be found like Brutus, like himself.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. This is not Brutus, friend; but, I assure you,
A prize no less in worth. Keep this man safe,
Give him all kindness. I had rather have
Such men my friends than enemies. Go on,
And see whether Brutus be alive or dead;
And bring us word unto Octavius’ tent
How everything is chanc’d.
paras.t: This is not Brutus, friend; but, I assure you, A prize no less in worth. Keep this man safe, Give him all kindness. I had rather have Such men my friends than enemies. Go on, And see whether Brutus be alive or dead; And bring us word unto Octavius’ tent How everything is chanc’d.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.

chapters.sub: Scene V · Another part of the field

paras.html: Enter Brutus, Dardanius, Clitus, Strato and Volumnius.
paras.t: Enter Brutus, Dardanius, Clitus, Strato and Volumnius.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Come, poor remains of friends, rest on this rock.
paras.t: Come, poor remains of friends, rest on this rock.

paras.html:
CLITUS. Statilius show’d the torch-light; but, my lord,
He came not back: he is or ta’en or slain.
paras.t: Statilius show’d the torch-light; but, my lord, He came not back: he is or ta’en or slain.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Sit thee down, Clitus. Slaying is the word;
It is a deed in fashion. Hark thee, Clitus.
paras.t: Sit thee down, Clitus. Slaying is the word; It is a deed in fashion. Hark thee, Clitus.

paras.html: Whispering.
paras.t: Whispering.

paras.html: CLITUS. What, I, my lord? No, not for all the world.
paras.t: What, I, my lord? No, not for all the world.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Peace then, no words.
paras.t: Peace then, no words.

paras.html: CLITUS. I’ll rather kill myself.
paras.t: I’ll rather kill myself.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Hark thee, Dardanius.
paras.t: Hark thee, Dardanius.

paras.html: Whispers him.
paras.t: Whispers him.

paras.html: DARDANIUS. Shall I do such a deed?
paras.t: Shall I do such a deed?

paras.html: CLITUS. O Dardanius!
paras.t: O Dardanius!

paras.html: DARDANIUS. O Clitus!
paras.t: O Clitus!

paras.html: CLITUS. What ill request did Brutus make to thee?
paras.t: What ill request did Brutus make to thee?

paras.html: DARDANIUS. To kill him, Clitus. Look, he meditates.
paras.t: To kill him, Clitus. Look, he meditates.

paras.html:
CLITUS. Now is that noble vessel full of grief,
That it runs over even at his eyes.
paras.t: Now is that noble vessel full of grief, That it runs over even at his eyes.

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Come hither, good Volumnius; list a word.
paras.t: Come hither, good Volumnius; list a word.

paras.html: VOLUMNIUS. What says my lord?
paras.t: What says my lord?

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Why, this, Volumnius:
The ghost of Caesar hath appear’d to me
Two several times by night; at Sardis once,
And this last night here in Philippi fields.
I know my hour is come.
paras.t: Why, this, Volumnius: The ghost of Caesar hath appear’d to me Two several times by night; at Sardis once, And this last night here in Philippi fields. I know my hour is come.

paras.html: VOLUMNIUS. Not so, my lord.
paras.t: Not so, my lord.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Nay I am sure it is, Volumnius.
Thou seest the world, Volumnius, how it goes;
Our enemies have beat us to the pit.
paras.t: Nay I am sure it is, Volumnius. Thou seest the world, Volumnius, how it goes; Our enemies have beat us to the pit.

paras.html: Low alarums.
paras.t: Low alarums.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. It is more worthy to leap in ourselves
Than tarry till they push us. Good Volumnius,
Thou know’st that we two went to school together;
Even for that our love of old, I pr’ythee
Hold thou my sword-hilts, whilst I run on it.
paras.t: It is more worthy to leap in ourselves Than tarry till they push us. Good Volumnius, Thou know’st that we two went to school together; Even for that our love of old, I pr’ythee Hold thou my sword-hilts, whilst I run on it.

paras.html: VOLUMNIUS. That’s not an office for a friend, my lord.
paras.t: That’s not an office for a friend, my lord.

paras.html: Alarums still.
paras.t: Alarums still.

paras.html: CLITUS. Fly, fly, my lord! there is no tarrying here.
paras.t: Fly, fly, my lord! there is no tarrying here.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Farewell to you; and you; and you, Volumnius.
Strato, thou hast been all this while asleep;
Farewell to thee too, Strato.—Countrymen,
My heart doth joy, that yet in all my life
I found no man but he was true to me.
I shall have glory by this losing day
More than Octavius and Mark Antony
By this vile conquest shall attain unto.
So fare you well at once; for Brutus’ tongue
Hath almost ended his life’s history.
Night hangs upon mine eyes; my bones would rest,
That have but labour’d to attain this hour.
paras.t: Farewell to you; and you; and you, Volumnius. Strato, thou hast been all this while asleep; Farewell to thee too, Strato.—Countrymen, My heart doth joy, that yet in all my life I found no man but he was true to me. I shall have glory by this losing day More than Octavius and Mark Antony By this vile conquest shall attain unto. So fare you well at once; for Brutus’ tongue Hath almost ended his life’s history. Night hangs upon mine eyes; my bones would rest, That have but labour’d to attain this hour.

paras.html: Alarums. Cry within, “Fly, fly, fly!”.
paras.t: Alarums. Cry within, “Fly, fly, fly!”.

paras.html: CLITUS. Fly, my lord, fly!
paras.t: Fly, my lord, fly!

paras.html: MARCUS BRUTUS. Hence! I will follow.
paras.t: Hence! I will follow.

paras.html: Exeunt Clitus, Dardanius and Volumnius.
paras.t: Exeunt Clitus, Dardanius and Volumnius.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. I pr’ythee, Strato, stay thou by thy lord.
Thou art a fellow of a good respect;
Thy life hath had some smatch of honour in it.
Hold then my sword, and turn away thy face,
While I do run upon it. Wilt thou, Strato?
paras.t: I pr’ythee, Strato, stay thou by thy lord. Thou art a fellow of a good respect; Thy life hath had some smatch of honour in it. Hold then my sword, and turn away thy face, While I do run upon it. Wilt thou, Strato?

paras.html: STRATO. Give me your hand first. Fare you well, my lord.
paras.t: Give me your hand first. Fare you well, my lord.

paras.html:
MARCUS BRUTUS. Farewell, good Strato.—Caesar, now be still:
I kill’d not thee with half so good a will.
paras.t: Farewell, good Strato.—Caesar, now be still: I kill’d not thee with half so good a will.

paras.html: He runs on his sword, and dies.
paras.t: He runs on his sword, and dies.

paras.html: Alarum. Retreat. Enter Antony, Octavius, Messala, Lucilius and the Army.
paras.t: Alarum. Retreat. Enter Antony, Octavius, Messala, Lucilius and the Army.

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. What man is that?
paras.t: What man is that?

paras.html: MESSALA. My master’s man. Strato, where is thy master?
paras.t: My master’s man. Strato, where is thy master?

paras.html:
STRATO. Free from the bondage you are in, Messala.
The conquerors can but make a fire of him;
For Brutus only overcame himself,
And no man else hath honour by his death.
paras.t: Free from the bondage you are in, Messala. The conquerors can but make a fire of him; For Brutus only overcame himself, And no man else hath honour by his death.

paras.html:
LUCILIUS. So Brutus should be found. I thank thee, Brutus,
That thou hast prov’d Lucilius’ saying true.
paras.t: So Brutus should be found. I thank thee, Brutus, That thou hast prov’d Lucilius’ saying true.

paras.html:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR. All that serv’d Brutus, I will entertain them.
Fellow, wilt thou bestow thy time with me?
paras.t: All that serv’d Brutus, I will entertain them. Fellow, wilt thou bestow thy time with me?

paras.html: STRATO. Ay, if Messala will prefer me to you.
paras.t: Ay, if Messala will prefer me to you.

paras.html: OCTAVIUS CAESAR. Do so, good Messala.
paras.t: Do so, good Messala.

paras.html: MESSALA. How died my master, Strato?
paras.t: How died my master, Strato?

paras.html: STRATO. I held the sword, and he did run on it.
paras.t: I held the sword, and he did run on it.

paras.html:
MESSALA. Octavius, then take him to follow thee,
That did the latest service to my master.
paras.t: Octavius, then take him to follow thee, That did the latest service to my master.

paras.html:
MARK ANTONY. This was the noblest Roman of them all.
All the conspirators save only he,
Did that they did in envy of great Caesar;
He only, in a general honest thought
And common good to all, made one of them.
His life was gentle, and the elements
So mix’d in him that Nature might stand up
And say to all the world, “This was a man!”
paras.t: This was the noblest Roman of them all. All the conspirators save only he, Did that they did in envy of great Caesar; He only, in a general honest thought And common good to all, made one of them. His life was gentle, and the elements So mix’d in him that Nature might stand up And say to all the world, “This was a man!”

paras.html:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR. According to his virtue let us use him
With all respect and rites of burial.
Within my tent his bones tonight shall lie,
Most like a soldier, order’d honourably.
So call the field to rest, and let’s away,
To part the glories of this happy day.
paras.t: According to his virtue let us use him With all respect and rites of burial. Within my tent his bones tonight shall lie, Most like a soldier, order’d honourably. So call the field to rest, and let’s away, To part the glories of this happy day.

paras.html: Exeunt.
paras.t: Exeunt.
